A.G. File No. 2025-016
October 20, 2025
PDF Version (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250421.pdf)
Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed constitutional initiative that maintains personal income tax rates for high-income taxpayers (A.G. File No. 25-0016).
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Personal Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for the majority of spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Recent Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend This Money? The state collects taxes from people and businesses and uses them to pay for services to the public. This year, the state plans to spend about $230 billion from the General Fund. About half of this spending is for K-12 schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The amount spent on K-12 schools and community colleges is set by the State Constitution.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's health insurance program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, parole programs, and courts.
Proposal
This measure maintains the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 by making them permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Measure Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by this measure is hard to predict and will go up and down with the economy. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing investment income and capital gains. These types of income are closely tied to the stock market and therefore go up and down a lot from year to year. In a weak year, the measure might bring in around $5 billion in revenue. In a strong year, the measure might bring in $15 billion in annual revenue. In most years, revenue brought in by the measure would be in between these amounts. These amounts are in today's dollars and would tend to grow over time.
A Large Portion of the Money Would Go to Schools and Community Colleges. The State Constitution requires the state to spend a large portion of new money on schools and community colleges. Typically, about 40 percent of the revenue brought in by this measure would go to schools and community colleges.
A Smaller Portion of the Money Would Go to Reserves. The State Constitution requires the state to set aside money to save in budget reserves. Reserves help the state balance its budget when the economy is weak and revenues decline. Some of the money brought in under this measure would be saved in reserves. This means the state would have more money in savings to balance the budget when the economy is weak.
Remaining Money Could Be Spent on Other State Programs. Money brought in under this measure that does not go to schools, community colleges, or reserves could be used for other state programs.
Summary of Fiscal Effects. We estimate the measure would have the following major fiscal effects:
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income taxes (in today's dollars) by making a tax on high income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

Let me look at the opposing side arguments more carefully: San Diego Union-Tribune editorial (no), OC Register editorial (no), CalMatters commentary against, and also research on revenue volatility and migration effects. Also, key issue: the "conflicting measures" clause in Prop 3 — does it affect Prop 40/41/42? Let's check news coverage on that.

Also, one nuance: Prop 3's text apparently doesn't actually "guarantee" funds directly to schools in a new way; it makes permanent Prop 30's Education Protection Account provisions. Wait — under Prop 55, the revenue did NOT go into the Education Protection Account; Prop 55 revenues went to the General Fund with Prop 98 formula. Prop 30 had the Education Protection Account with 89%/11% split and the healthcare carve-out (50% of excess above Prop 98 minimum + workload budget, up to $2B, to DHCS). Prop 3 appears to restore/permanently extend Article XIII Section 36 as originally written in Prop 30 (amending the sunset dates). So the Education Protection Account mechanism would be permanent: 89% K-12, 11% CCC, up to $2B to children's Medi-Cal.

Hmm, but note that the LAO says roughly 40% goes to schools and community colleges. That's because revenue counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee, so the Education Protection Account funds are largely counted as part of Prop 98 minimum — meaning the extra money to schools beyond what Prop 98 requires is smaller. Actually, the EPA allocation mechanism gives 89/11 of revenues to schools/community colleges as "general purpose funding" which counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee; the state must still meet the guarantee from other funds. Net effect: schools get about 40% of revenue per LAO (the Prop 98 minimum share). This is an important nuance where the proponents' claim "funds go directly to classrooms" is partly true mechanically but the net fiscal benefit to schools is ~40%.

Also there's the interaction with Prop 98: making revenue permanent raises the Prop 98 guarantee permanently, reducing flexibility. Also the volatility issue: high-income tax revenues are volatile; permanent reliance deepens volatility. Though Prop 2 (rainy day fund) is also on the ballot, which would strengthen reserves.

Consider migration/economic effects: PPIC and others find minimal migration effect for the top 2% from Prop 30/55 — CA has had second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households. But some argue permanence at a time when other states cut taxes and federal tax changes (OBBBA raising SALT cap to $40k) change the calculus. The 13.3% top rate (with mental health surtax) is highest in nation; combined with federal, high earners in CA face ~50%+ marginal rates. There's evidence of modest elasticity among top earners (Kleven/Landais: small but non-zero migration elasticity for top earners; more relevant: capital gains timing/realization shifts). Also 2024's Prop 2? Not relevant.

Let me also check the "conflicting measures" clause analysis — this is a significant consideration. If Prop 3 passes with more votes than Prop 40, does Prop 40 get nullified? Prop 40 is a one-time excise tax on net worth, not a "tax rate for personal income," so probably not a conflict. But Props 41 and 42 (billionaire countermeasures) — Prop 41 (tax audits) and Prop 42 (prohibits new state property taxes)? Let me look at what these are. The LA Times said "Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40 from becoming law even if voters pass it." Hmm. Prop 3's conflicting-measure clause could nullify Prop 41/42 if Prop 3 gets more votes — but that only matters if they conflict on "tax rates for personal income."

Let me search for analysis of Prop 3's conflicting measures provision and the interaction with Prop 40/41/42. Also, let me get the SDUT and OC Register editorials for the "no" case in full, plus the CalMatters commentary against.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

Both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, the most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years, saw evaluating teacher effectiveness as a much-needed education reform. This shows Clinton walking with then-President Obama as they golfed in Maryland in 2011. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

Let me look at the opposing side arguments more carefully: San Diego Union-Tribune editorial (no), OC Register editorial (no), CalMatters commentary against, and also research on revenue volatility and migration effects. Also, key issue: the "conflicting measures" clause in Prop 3 — does it affect Prop 40/41/42? Let's check news coverage on that.

Also, one nuance: Prop 3's text apparently doesn't actually "guarantee" funds directly to schools in a new way; it makes permanent Prop 30's Education Protection Account provisions. Wait — under Prop 55, the revenue did NOT go into the Education Protection Account; Prop 55 revenues went to the General Fund with Prop 98 formula. Prop 30 had the Education Protection Account with 89%/11% split and the healthcare carve-out (50% of excess above Prop 98 minimum + workload budget, up to $2B, to DHCS). Prop 3 appears to restore/permanently extend Article XIII Section 36 as originally written in Prop 30 (amending the sunset dates). So the Education Protection Account mechanism would be permanent: 89% K-12, 11% CCC, up to $2B to children's Medi-Cal.

Hmm, but note that the LAO says roughly 40% goes to schools and community colleges. That's because revenue counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee, so the Education Protection Account funds are largely counted as part of Prop 98 minimum — meaning the extra money to schools beyond what Prop 98 requires is smaller. Actually, the EPA allocation mechanism gives 89/11 of revenues to schools/community colleges as "general purpose funding" which counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee; the state must still meet the guarantee from other funds. Net effect: schools get about 40% of revenue per LAO (the Prop 98 minimum share). This is an important nuance where the proponents' claim "funds go directly to classrooms" is partly true mechanically but the net fiscal benefit to schools is ~40%.

Also there's the interaction with Prop 98: making revenue permanent raises the Prop 98 guarantee permanently, reducing flexibility. Also the volatility issue: high-income tax revenues are volatile; permanent reliance deepens volatility. Though Prop 2 (rainy day fund) is also on the ballot, which would strengthen reserves.

Consider migration/economic effects: PPIC and others find minimal migration effect for the top 2% from Prop 30/55 — CA has had second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households. But some argue permanence at a time when other states cut taxes and federal tax changes (OBBBA raising SALT cap to $40k) change the calculus. The 13.3% top rate (with mental health surtax) is highest in nation; combined with federal, high earners in CA face ~50%+ marginal rates. There's evidence of modest elasticity among top earners (Kleven/Landais: small but non-zero migration elasticity for top earners; more relevant: capital gains timing/realization shifts). Also 2024's Prop 2? Not relevant.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

Interesting nuance: Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause vs. Props 40/41/42. And tax law professors note Prop 42 might undermine Prop 3. But Prop 3 has its own conflict clause: if Prop 3 gets more yes votes than a conflicting measure affecting personal income tax rates, Prop 3 prevails. Prop 3 polls at 54-58% yes; Prop 41/42 poll around 50-51%. So Prop 3 likely gets more yes votes than 41/42 → Prop 3 would prevail over them if deemed conflicting. That's a legal question.

Now, for a decision, let me weigh:

Pro-yes considerations:
1. Revenue: $5-15B/year, essential to state budget; expiry would force ~$10B+ in cuts or new taxes.
2. Rates only affect top 2%; no tax increase relative to current law (though relative to what would otherwise happen after 2031, it is an increase).
3. Empirical evidence: minimal migration effect from Prop 30/55 over 14 years; CA out-migration among high earners is low; PPIC data.
4. Federal cuts (H.R. 1) to Medi-Cal create new funding needs; Prop 3 backfills up to $2B/year for children's healthcare.
5. Accountability provisions: Education Protection Account, no administrative costs, annual audits, online posting.
6. Broad support: teachers, nurses, PTA, CMA, Democratic Party; editorial boards SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee; SPUR yes; polls 54-58% yes.
7. Progressive tax structure: revenue volatility is partly mitigated by rainy day fund; and Prop 2 on same ballot strengthens reserves.

Pro-no considerations:
1. Permanence locks in the state's highest-in-nation top marginal rate (13.3% with MHST), reducing future flexibility; makes structural reliance on volatile capital gains revenue permanent.
2. "Temporary" promise broken; precedent of moving goalposts.
3. No urgency — the tax doesn't expire until end of 2030; the Legislature/voters could decide in 2028 or 2030 with better information; deciding now forgoes leverage for reform (e.g., school accountability, cost control).
4. California's affordability crisis and out-migration of lower/middle-income residents; high taxes on top earners arguably contribute to cost of living, business climate; risk that permanence accelerates departure of high earners, especially combined with Prop 40 uncertainty and federal SALT cap changes.
5. Declining K-12 enrollment: spending per pupil at record high while outcomes remain mediocre; permanent dedication of revenue reduces flexibility to reallocate.
6. The initiative's dedication to the EPA and the conflict clause may interact with other measures (Props 41/42) creating legal uncertainty.
7. Constitutional amendments that permanently dedicate revenue are generally considered bad budget practice (LAO has criticized "lockbox" measures and rigidity).

Now, which is "better"? Let me think about the strongest analytical considerations. Let me dig a bit more into the migration evidence and the fiscal impact of letting it expire. Also, whether the state would actually cut $10B or replace it. And the LAO's assessment of Prop 98 implications: if revenue falls, Prop 98 minimum falls too, so cuts to schools would be moderated. The LAO's analysis says roughly 40% to schools.

Consider also: is it better policy to make the rate permanent vs. letting it expire and possibly replacing with a broader tax? California's income tax reliance on top earners is extreme (top 1% pay ~40-50% of income tax). Volatility caused big swings (2023 $30B+ shortfall driven by capital gains). Permanence entrenches that. But the counterargument: the rates already exist through 2030, and the state budget now structurally depends on them; letting them lapse would force deep cuts or new taxes at a worse time. There's no serious proposal to replace them with a less volatile tax.

Also, note the fiscal context in 2026: California has deficits and federal cuts to Medi-Cal. If Prop 3 fails, the state loses $5-15B annually starting 2031, which would be roughly a 4-6% General Fund cut.

Let me look at a few more sources: the CalMatters "What to know about Prop 3" article, the LA Times guide, and the opposition commentary (CalMatters commentary against). Also check whether any credible centrist group (e.g., PPIC, Bay Area Council, Chamber of Commerce) opposed. And the "Yes on 3" funding sources (CTA). Also check any analysis of whether Prop 3 could cause wealth managers/high earners to relocate — e.g., evidence from New Jersey's millionaire tax, from California's Prop 30 studies.

If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. An income tax on California’s highest earners, first passed in 2012, will expire in five years unless voters make the levy for school funding permanent. Below, an anti-tax advocate argues California’s pattern of making temporary taxes permanent is bad policy, and voters can break the cycle. The opposing view: A cafeteria manager says students and families will be hit hardest (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) if Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) fails. Guest Commentary written by Robert Gutierrez Robert Gutierrez is president of the California Taxpayers Association. For more than a century, California’s tax system has followed a familiar pattern: A fiscal crisis emerges, government responds with a “temporary” tax increase, the crisis passes and the tax remains. Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would continue this troubling pattern by making a “temporary” tax increase permanent. Supporters of Prop. 3 argue that the measure will provide ongoing funding for two priorities of most Californians, education and healthcare. The question is not whether those services matter — clearly, they do — but whether it is a sound policy to permanently extend tax hikes that voters were repeatedly told would expire. When California voters approved higher personal income tax rates in 2012, they were told the increase was a short-term emergency response to a specific fiscal challenge. Four years later, voters were asked to extend the tax increases, again for a limited time. Prop. 3 would make the tax hikes permanent — during a year in which high taxes and the unaffordable cost of living are the biggest problems for the majority of Californians. A recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) found that roughly half of Californians say the cost of living is their top concern, and 55% prefer lower taxes and fewer government services. The reason that “temporary” tax hikes rarely disappear is that once government adjusts its spending to the higher revenue, politicians and special interests treat this as the new baseline. It doesn’t have to be this way. By rejecting Prop. 3, California voters can break the tradition and make sure that a temporary tax truly is temporary. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Proposition 3 sustains California schools. Losing the high-income tax would be devastating (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) It is worth noting that California’s new state budget establishes record-high education spending of $27,418 per pupil (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/TK-12Education.pdf), up 27% from just five years earlier (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2021-22/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/K-12Education.pdf). Public schools continue to be the state’s top priority, receiving roughly 46% of the state’s general fund budget (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/SummaryCharts.pdf). Additionally, the entire budget reached a record high of $351.7 billion in spending, an $89 billion increase in spending (34%) from five years ago. In other words, any fiscal emergency of the past has been addressed. Supporters characterize Prop. 3 as affecting only high-income taxpayers, but it is not that simple. California’s tax system does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S corporations, reporting business earnings on personal income tax returns. As a result, extending higher tax rates would sustain higher costs for many small businesses — ultimately resulting in higher prices for their customers. The broader economic effects deserve scrutiny, as well. California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and has the highest state sales tax rate and gas tax. The state applies an additional 1.3% tax on all wage income to pay for the State Disability Insurance program. In addition to keeping costs high in California, Prop. 3 would deepen California’s reliance on the state’s most volatile revenue source: taxes paid by high-income earners (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/#5dfdd7c1-ccba-4770-802a-ec01052bfd71). During economic expansions, revenue surges. During downturns, revenue can fall dramatically, leaving the state struggling to pay ongoing expenses — especially when the demand for public services is increasing. Expanding permanent spending commitments tied to the most volatile revenue stream reduces flexibility when the economy weakens. Education and healthcare deserve stable funding. But stable funding should rest on honest budgeting and prioritizing the ample resources already available — not on repeatedly extending taxes that voters were assured would expire. If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. Interesting nuance: Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause vs. Props 40/41/42. And tax law professors note Prop 42 might undermine Prop 3. But Prop 3 has its own conflict clause: if Prop 3 gets more yes votes than a conflicting measure affecting personal income tax rates, Prop 3 prevails. Prop 3 polls at 54-58% yes; Prop 41/42 poll around 50-51%. So Prop 3 likely gets more yes votes than 41/42 → Prop 3 would prevail over them if deemed conflicting. That's a legal question.

Now, for a decision, let me weigh:

Pro-yes considerations:
1. Revenue: $5-15B/year, essential to state budget; expiry would force ~$10B+ in cuts or new taxes.
2. Rates only affect top 2%; no tax increase relative to current law (though relative to what would otherwise happen after 2031, it is an increase).
3. Empirical evidence: minimal migration effect from Prop 30/55 over 14 years; CA out-migration among high earners is low; PPIC data.
4. Federal cuts (H.R. 1) to Medi-Cal create new funding needs; Prop 3 backfills up to $2B/year for children's healthcare.
5. Accountability provisions: Education Protection Account, no administrative costs, annual audits, online posting.
6. Broad support: teachers, nurses, PTA, CMA, Democratic Party; editorial boards SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee; SPUR yes; polls 54-58% yes.
7. Progressive tax structure: revenue volatility is partly mitigated by rainy day fund; and Prop 2 on same ballot strengthens reserves.

Pro-no considerations:
1. Permanence locks in the state's highest-in-nation top marginal rate (13.3% with MHST), reducing future flexibility; makes structural reliance on volatile capital gains revenue permanent.
2. "Temporary" promise broken; precedent of moving goalposts.
3. No urgency — the tax doesn't expire until end of 2030; the Legislature/voters could decide in 2028 or 2030 with better information; deciding now forgoes leverage for reform (e.g., school accountability, cost control).
4. California's affordability crisis and out-migration of lower/middle-income residents; high taxes on top earners arguably contribute to cost of living, business climate; risk that permanence accelerates departure of high earners, especially combined with Prop 40 uncertainty and federal SALT cap changes.
5. Declining K-12 enrollment: spending per pupil at record high while outcomes remain mediocre; permanent dedication of revenue reduces flexibility to reallocate.
6. The initiative's dedication to the EPA and the conflict clause may interact with other measures (Props 41/42) creating legal uncertainty.
7. Constitutional amendments that permanently dedicate revenue are generally considered bad budget practice (LAO has criticized "lockbox" measures and rigidity).

Now, which is "better"? Let me think about the strongest analytical considerations. Let me dig a bit more into the migration evidence and the fiscal impact of letting it expire. Also, whether the state would actually cut $10B or replace it. And the LAO's assessment of Prop 98 implications: if revenue falls, Prop 98 minimum falls too, so cuts to schools would be moderated. The LAO's analysis says roughly 40% to schools.

Consider also: is it better policy to make the rate permanent vs. letting it expire and possibly replacing with a broader tax? California's income tax reliance on top earners is extreme (top 1% pay ~40-50% of income tax). Volatility caused big swings (2023 $30B+ shortfall driven by capital gains). Permanence entrenches that. But the counterargument: the rates already exist through 2030, and the state budget now structurally depends on them; letting them lapse would force deep cuts or new taxes at a worse time. There's no serious proposal to replace them with a less volatile tax.

Also, note the fiscal context in 2026: California has deficits and federal cuts to Medi-Cal. If Prop 3 fails, the state loses $5-15B annually starting 2031, which would be roughly a 4-6% General Fund cut.

Let me look at a few more sources: the CalMatters "What to know about Prop 3" article, the LA Times guide, and the opposition commentary (CalMatters commentary against). Also check whether any credible centrist group (e.g., PPIC, Bay Area Council, Chamber of Commerce) opposed. And the "Yes on 3" funding sources (CTA). Also check any analysis of whether Prop 3 could cause wealth managers/high earners to relocate — e.g., evidence from New Jersey's millionaire tax, from California's Prop 30 studies.

Let me fetch the CalMatters commentary against and the CalMatters Prop 3 explainer.

Only two weeks into the school year, students are doing basic exercises to familiarize themselves with lab instruments, learn the value of accuracy, and practice working together to build a foundation for the rest of the year. Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters In summary Voters first passed the tax in 2012, then renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. An income tax on California’s highest earners, first passed in 2012, will expire in five years unless voters make the levy for school funding permanent. Below, an anti-tax advocate argues California’s pattern of making temporary taxes permanent is bad policy, and voters can break the cycle. The opposing view: A cafeteria manager says students and families will be hit hardest (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) if Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) fails. Guest Commentary written by Robert Gutierrez Robert Gutierrez is president of the California Taxpayers Association. For more than a century, California’s tax system has followed a familiar pattern: A fiscal crisis emerges, government responds with a “temporary” tax increase, the crisis passes and the tax remains. Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would continue this troubling pattern by making a “temporary” tax increase permanent. Supporters of Prop. 3 argue that the measure will provide ongoing funding for two priorities of most Californians, education and healthcare. The question is not whether those services matter — clearly, they do — but whether it is a sound policy to permanently extend tax hikes that voters were repeatedly told would expire. When California voters approved higher personal income tax rates in 2012, they were told the increase was a short-term emergency response to a specific fiscal challenge. Four years later, voters were asked to extend the tax increases, again for a limited time. Prop. 3 would make the tax hikes permanent — during a year in which high taxes and the unaffordable cost of living are the biggest problems for the majority of Californians. A recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) found that roughly half of Californians say the cost of living is their top concern, and 55% prefer lower taxes and fewer government services. The reason that “temporary” tax hikes rarely disappear is that once government adjusts its spending to the higher revenue, politicians and special interests treat this as the new baseline. It doesn’t have to be this way. By rejecting Prop. 3, California voters can break the tradition and make sure that a temporary tax truly is temporary. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Proposition 3 sustains California schools. Losing the high-income tax would be devastating (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) It is worth noting that California’s new state budget establishes record-high education spending of $27,418 per pupil (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/TK-12Education.pdf), up 27% from just five years earlier (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2021-22/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/K-12Education.pdf). Public schools continue to be the state’s top priority, receiving roughly 46% of the state’s general fund budget (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/SummaryCharts.pdf). Additionally, the entire budget reached a record high of $351.7 billion in spending, an $89 billion increase in spending (34%) from five years ago. In other words, any fiscal emergency of the past has been addressed. Supporters characterize Prop. 3 as affecting only high-income taxpayers, but it is not that simple. California’s tax system does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S corporations, reporting business earnings on personal income tax returns. As a result, extending higher tax rates would sustain higher costs for many small businesses — ultimately resulting in higher prices for their customers. The broader economic effects deserve scrutiny, as well. California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and has the highest state sales tax rate and gas tax. The state applies an additional 1.3% tax on all wage income to pay for the State Disability Insurance program. In addition to keeping costs high in California, Prop. 3 would deepen California’s reliance on the state’s most volatile revenue source: taxes paid by high-income earners (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/#5dfdd7c1-ccba-4770-802a-ec01052bfd71). During economic expansions, revenue surges. During downturns, revenue can fall dramatically, leaving the state struggling to pay ongoing expenses — especially when the demand for public services is increasing. Expanding permanent spending commitments tied to the most volatile revenue stream reduces flexibility when the economy weakens. Education and healthcare deserve stable funding. But stable funding should rest on honest budgeting and prioritizing the ample resources already available — not on repeatedly extending taxes that voters were assured would expire. Good — this is a genuinely contested empirical question. Rauh/Shyu find meaningful behavioral erosion (~45-56% of expected windfall revenue eroded in first years, and 0.8pp increase in departure rate for the top bracket), while Varner/Young/Prohofsky find little migration response. Note that even if revenue eroded 45-56%, the tax still raised substantial revenue ($104B+ cumulative per proponents; Controller's tracking site). So the behavioral response reduces but doesn't eliminate revenue. And notably, the "erosion" estimate means the state collects roughly half of the static estimate — which is still $5-10B/yr.

Also important: LAO's estimates of $5-15B presumably account for some behavioral response? Not necessarily.

Now, the state's fiscal situation: LAO projects structural deficits of $20-35 billion annually starting 2027-28. In that context, letting $5-15B of revenue lapse in 2031 would deepen the structural gap; alternatively, a "no" vote gives the Legislature pressure to reform spending. Note that the LAO says the problem is structural — spending growth outstrips revenue growth — and even with record PIT revenues there are deficits. Hmm, that's an argument that Prop 3 alone doesn't solve the structural problem, but it doesn't follow that losing $10B/year would help.

One important nuance: Because of Prop 98 and Prop 2 (2014), revenue increases get largely offset by constitutionally required spending on schools and reserves — LAO noted "constitutional spending requirements under Proposition 98 and Proposition 2 almost entirely offset revenue gains." So a "yes" vote keeps $5-15B, but roughly 40%+ goes to schools automatically, ~some to reserves, and the rest to other programs. If the tax expires, Prop 98 minimum would decline correspondingly, meaning schools would absorb ~40% of the loss through the formula, so the hit to the rest of the budget would be ~60% of the loss. Still large.

Let me consider the strongest arguments:

Yes case:
- The state faces a structural deficit; losing $5-15B/yr (about 4-6% of General Fund) starting in 2031 would force deep cuts to education, healthcare, and other services, or new broad-based taxes. Given federal Medicaid cuts (H.R. 1) hitting California (estimated $30B/yr loss to Medi-Cal per SFGate), the fiscal need is acute.
- The tax is highly progressive, hitting only top 2%, who pay about half of income tax. Empirical evidence on migration is mixed but the tax has been in place 14 years without an exodus; PPIC finds those leaving CA are less affluent than those moving in; CBPP finds state taxes have minimal impact on interstate moves.
- No new tax: rates stay as they've been since 2013. Voting no means a tax cut for the top 2% of ~$10B/yr that the state cannot afford.
- Accountability: EPA dedicated 89/11 to K-12/CCC, no admin costs, audits.
- Broad coalition support (CTA, PTA, CMA, nurses, firefighters, CA Democratic Party); most major editorial boards in favor; polls 54-58% yes.

No case:
- Permanence eliminates voter/legislative leverage; temporary taxes force periodic reevaluation. There's no urgency since expiration is 2031; a decision could be deferred to 2028/2030 (and if it fails now, proponents can re-qualify).
- Deepens reliance on the most volatile revenue source at a moment when LAO warns of a stock-market bubble and structural deficits; permanence reduces budget flexibility.
- California's top rate 13.3% is the highest in the nation; combined with federal and other taxes it's near the top globally; evidence (Rauh/Shyu) of behavioral erosion, which is a real cost, plus risk of accelerating out-migration of high earners and entrepreneurs, especially given Prop 40's chilling effect and other states (Texas, Florida, Nevada, Washington) recruiting businesses.
- Small business pass-through income is affected (S-corps, partnerships), raising costs for businesses and consumers.
- Spending per pupil is at a record high ($27,418) while outcomes remain mediocre; enrollment declining ~500k students; no reforms attached to the money. Locking in funding without accountability for results (SDUT argument).
- The initiative's rigid dedication reduces the Legislature's flexibility, and the conflict clause adds legal uncertainty interacting with Props 40/41/42.

How to weigh? Consider a median-voter/public-interest framework. Key considerations:

1. Is the revenue needed? Almost certainly yes given structural deficits and federal cuts. But "no" doesn't automatically mean revenue disappears — it could be re-authorized in 2028 or 2030. However, waiting creates uncertainty for school budgeting and would likely trigger preemptive cuts before 2031. Also, history shows extension measures passed comfortably in 2016 (63%). So the practical difference between yes now and yes in 2030 is mostly about timing certainty and the political capital spent.

2. Is permanence bad? Per se, permanence of a well-functioning, highly progressive tax that has not caused a measurable exodus is not obviously harmful. However, budget scholars (LAO) have long criticized ballot-box budgeting and rigid dedications. But Prop 3's dedication is essentially the same mechanism as Prop 30's, already in place.

3. Volatility: A real concern, but Prop 3 does route excess to reserves; and the alternative (expiry) doesn't reduce volatility of the remaining tax base — California's PIT concentration exists regardless. Actually, allowing rates to revert to 9.3% would reduce revenue concentration somewhat but not much.

4. Equity/economic efficiency: The tax burden falls on high earners and capital gains. Efficiency costs (behavioral response) exist but are modest relative to the revenue raised, and the revenue funds education — which has high social returns, especially for low-income students (LCFF). Education spending increases have been shown to improve outcomes (Jackson et al.), though California's outcomes remain weak.

5. The "tax flight" argument: mixed evidence; but the Rauh findings, even if true, imply revenue erosion not revenue loss; and CA's top earners' departure rate ~2% vs 1.5% baseline is small. Also, note that under Prop 3 rates don't change, so no new marginal incentive to leave relative to today; only relative to a counterfactual where rates drop to 9.3%. So a "no" vote could bring some high earners back/keep them, generating some economic benefit, but also forfeit $5-15B in revenue.

6. Also important: the political economy. If Prop 3 fails, will the Legislature replace the revenue with a broader, more stable tax (e.g., expanding sales tax to services)? Probably not; more likely deep cuts. Given LAO projects $20-35B structural deficits already, a further $10B revenue loss would likely be addressed with cuts to schools, healthcare, and other programs — harming lower-income Californians most. Meanwhile, beneficiaries of the tax cut are the top 2%.

Weighing the distributional and practical considerations: the measure preserves revenue that funds schools and healthcare, affects only the top 2%, changes no one's taxes relative to current law, and has strong institutional support. Opposition arguments are largely about principle (temporary means temporary), spending reform, and contested migration evidence, plus the loss of budget flexibility.

Counter-consideration: is the state's problem one of revenue or spending? LAO says structural: spending growth outstrips revenue growth. Adding permanent revenue doesn't fix the structural gap but it does reduce it (in 2031, revenue would drop). Actually if you reject Prop 3, revenue drops $5-15B in 2031 while Prop 98 spending requirements also drop ~40%, so the structural gap widens by roughly 60% of the loss — deepening deficits.

Hmm, but there's another angle: the LAO notes that revenue increases get "almost entirely offset" by Prop 98 and Prop 2 requirements — meaning the state's discretionary gain from new revenue is small. Conversely, losing revenue reduces required school spending automatically, so the discretionary hit is smaller than headline. Let me quantify: LAO says roughly 40% goes to schools/community colleges, some to reserves, rest to other programs. If the tax expires, the Prop 98 guarantee falls by roughly the school share, meaning schools would see reduced funding through the formula but the state's non-Prop 98 budget would lose ~60% ($3-9B) — still substantial.

Also note that in 2031, when it expires, the LAO says the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements (SPUR's phrasing) — over time Prop 98 minimum could decline.

- The revenue supports education and children's healthcare with meaningful accountability provisions.

But let me check a couple more things to be fair and thorough:
1. Is there any credible nonpartisan group opposing on grounds other than ideology (e.g., Bay Area Council, California Chamber of Commerce, PPIC)? Chamber of Commerce? Let me check who's on the no side beyond taxpayer groups: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association, Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, Howard Jarvis, Reform California. Also possibly some Democrats/moderate business groups? The LA Times said Prop 3 "garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Prop 40" — interesting, so some wealthy interests support Prop 3 as an alternative to Prop 40 (maybe to demonstrate revenue can be raised without a wealth tax; or because of the conflict clause).

2. Check whether there's a concern that Prop 3's conflict clause could nullify Prop 41/42 (which some voters might want). If Prop 3 gets more yes votes than Prop 41 or 42 and they're deemed conflicting (affecting "tax rates for personal income"), Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is null and void. Prop 41 concerns special taxes and Gann limit exemptions; Prop 42 concerns taxes on personal property. Arguably neither "affects the tax rates for personal income," though tax professors suggested Prop 42 could be read to nullify Prop 3 (a conflict). Under the constitutional rule, whichever gets more votes prevails. Prop 3 polls higher (54-58%) than 41/42 (~50%), so Prop 3 would likely prevail — meaning the Prop 3 clause could theoretically void Prop 41/42 entirely ("in their entirety"), which would be a consequential, possibly unintended effect: it would also remove Prop 41/42's nullification of Prop 40... hmm, actually if Prop 41/42 were void, then Prop 40 (if passed) would take effect. Interesting but speculative. Courts would decide. This is a real "hidden risk" consideration: voting yes on Prop 3 might inadvertently affect the billionaire-tax countermeasures. But that's speculative and probably minor; also many would see it as fine.

Let me quickly check the LA Times last-minute guide and the californiatoday guide for further "what's easy to miss" items about Prop 3, and see if any consumer-protection angle (e.g., whether Prop 3 contains a poison pill or unusual provisions like the proponent standing clause). Also check the SF Chronicle editorial for the yes case and whether it acknowledges downsides.

Let me do two more fetches: californiatoday.com guide and the LA Times last-minute guide.
