Counter-consideration: is the state's problem one of revenue or spending? LAO says structural: spending growth outstrips revenue growth. Adding permanent revenue doesn't fix the structural gap but it does reduce it (in 2031, revenue would drop). Actually if you reject Prop 3, revenue drops $5-15B in 2031 while Prop 98 spending requirements also drop ~40%, so the structural gap widens by roughly 60% of the loss — deepening deficits.

Hmm, but there's another angle: the LAO notes that revenue increases get "almost entirely offset" by Prop 98 and Prop 2 requirements — meaning the state's discretionary gain from new revenue is small. Conversely, losing revenue reduces required school spending automatically, so the discretionary hit is smaller than headline. Let me quantify: LAO says roughly 40% goes to schools/community colleges, some to reserves, rest to other programs. If the tax expires, the Prop 98 guarantee falls by roughly the school share, meaning schools would see reduced funding through the formula but the state's non-Prop 98 budget would lose ~60% ($3-9B) — still substantial.

Also note that in 2031, when it expires, the LAO says the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements (SPUR's phrasing) — over time Prop 98 minimum could decline.

I think the balance tips toward "yes," mainly because:
- The measure imposes no new tax and no rate increase relative to current law; it prevents a ~$10B/yr revenue loss concentrated as a tax cut for the top 2% at a time when the state faces structural deficits and federal Medicaid cuts.
- Empirical evidence on migration is mixed, and the burden of proof for a large economic harm is not met; PPIC/CBPP evidence and California's actual experience (14 years, $104-119B raised, high-earner out-migration low relative to other states) suggest the harm is modest.
- The revenue supports education and children's healthcare with meaningful accountability provisions.

But let me check a couple more things to be fair and thorough:
1. Is there any credible nonpartisan group opposing on grounds other than ideology (e.g., Bay Area Council, California Chamber of Commerce, PPIC)? Chamber of Commerce? Let me check who's on the no side beyond taxpayer groups: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association, Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, Howard Jarvis, Reform California. Also possibly some Democrats/moderate business groups? The LA Times said Prop 3 "garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Prop 40" — interesting, so some wealthy interests support Prop 3 as an alternative to Prop 40 (maybe to demonstrate revenue can be raised without a wealth tax; or because of the conflict clause).

2. Check whether there's a concern that Prop 3's conflict clause could nullify Prop 41/42 (which some voters might want). If Prop 3 gets more yes votes than Prop 41 or 42 and they're deemed conflicting (affecting "tax rates for personal income"), Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is null and void. Prop 41 concerns special taxes and Gann limit exemptions; Prop 42 concerns taxes on personal property. Arguably neither "affects the tax rates for personal income," though tax professors suggested Prop 42 could be read to nullify Prop 3 (a conflict). Under the constitutional rule, whichever gets more votes prevails. Prop 3 polls higher (54-58%) than 41/42 (~50%), so Prop 3 would likely prevail — meaning the Prop 3 clause could theoretically void Prop 41/42 entirely ("in their entirety"), which would be a consequential, possibly unintended effect: it would also remove Prop 41/42's nullification of Prop 40... hmm, actually if Prop 41/42 were void, then Prop 40 (if passed) would take effect. Interesting but speculative. Courts would decide. This is a real "hidden risk" consideration: voting yes on Prop 3 might inadvertently affect the billionaire-tax countermeasures. But that's speculative and probably minor; also many would see it as fine.

Let me quickly check the LA Times last-minute guide and the californiatoday guide for further "what's easy to miss" items about Prop 3, and see if any consumer-protection angle (e.g., whether Prop 3 contains a poison pill or unusual provisions like the proponent standing clause). Also check the SF Chronicle editorial for the yes case and whether it acknowledges downsides.

The "millionaire tax" is back on the California ballot: Proposition 3 would make the 2012 tax rates permanent
Proposition 3 would keep California's top income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% after 2030 instead of letting them drop to 9.3%. The brackets, what it means at $500,000 or $5 million, where the $5 billion to $15 billion goes, and who is paying for the campaign.

California's high-earner income tax is funding schools and community colleges under Proposition 3, which asks voters in November 2026 to make the 2012 rates permanent.
Proposition 3 would make California's highest income tax rates permanent. Since 2012, California's highest earners have paid 10.3%, 11.3% or 12.3% on the top slices of their income, rates that voters approved as Proposition 30 and extended as Proposition 55. Today those rates start at about $371,000 of taxable income for single filers and about $743,000 for joint filers. Those rates run through the 2030 tax year and then fall back to 9.3%. Prop 3, an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/) placed on the ballot by petition, deletes the end date; one of its two proponents is the president of the California Teachers Association. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it leads in both public polls: 58% to 40% in PPIC's September survey and 54% to 34% in UC Berkeley's.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The stakes are large and lopsided. The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates Prop 3 keeps $5 billion to $15 billion a year in the state budget, collected from the top 2% of taxpayers, who already pay about half of all state income taxes. Supporters frame a yes vote as no tax increase at all; opponents frame it as the "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." Both descriptions refer to the same rates. This explainer sets out what the text changes, what the rates mean in dollars, where the money goes (the 89% school figure and the LAO's 40% figure are both right, and measure different things), and who is paying for each side.
Proposition 3 deletes the 2030 end date from the Prop 30 tax rates

In the two paragraphs that set the higher rates, the words "and before January 1, 2031" are struck, so the rates apply "for any taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2012" with no end.
The line in each paragraph that says it "shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031" is struck.
In the rules for the Education Protection Account, the fund that receives the money, end years such as "2030" and "2030–31" become "thereafter."
The rates themselves are unchanged. In the Constitution they are written in 2012 dollars: 10.3% on single-filer income over $250,000, 11.3% over $300,000 and 12.3% over $500,000, with parallel brackets for heads of household, all "recomputed" each year for inflation under the state's normal indexing. The Franchise Tax Board's 2025 rate schedules (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-540-tax-rate-schedules.pdf) put those thresholds at $371,479, $445,771 and $742,953 for single filers; $742,958, $891,542 and $1,485,906 for joint filers; and $505,208, $606,251 and $1,010,417 for heads of household. Prop 3 does not touch the separate 1% tax on taxable income above $1 million that voters added for mental health services, now called the Behavioral Health Services Tax. Together the two make California's top marginal rate 13.3% today. If Prop 3 fails, the top rate in 2031 would be 10.3%.
The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure "that affects the tax rates for personal income" is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is void. The LAO's notes on potential interactions for Props 40, 41 and 42, the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) and its two countermeasures, do not mention Prop 3.
California income tax rates for top earners are holding at 10.3% to 12.3% under Proposition 3 rather than falling to 9.3% after 2030, with the yearly difference shown at incomes from $400,000 to $5 million in 2026. California income tax rates in dollars: $285 at $400,000, $134,398 at $5 million
The higher rates apply only to the slices of income above each threshold, so their effect starts small and grows quickly. Using the 2025 brackets, we calculated what the Prop 30 rates add to a year's state income tax compared with taxing the same income at 9.3% above the 9.3% threshold. A single filer with $400,000 of taxable income pays $285 more. At $500,000 the difference is $1,828; at $1 million, $14,398; at $5 million, $134,398. Joint filers' brackets are twice as wide: a couple with $500,000 pays nothing extra and a couple with $1 million pays $3,655 more, rising to $28,796 at $2 million and $118,796 at $5 million. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But there is another ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens that is getting far less attention — and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
The basics
Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) would make an expiring state income tax on high earners permanent.
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.

Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved. The state could expect to lose $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

The "millionaire tax" is back on the California ballot: Proposition 3 would make the 2012 tax rates permanent
Proposition 3 would keep California's top income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% after 2030 instead of letting them drop to 9.3%. The brackets, what it means at $500,000 or $5 million, where the $5 billion to $15 billion goes, and who is paying for the campaign.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 15, 2026

California's high-earner income tax is funding schools and community colleges under Proposition 3, which asks voters in November 2026 to make the 2012 rates permanent.
Proposition 3 would make California's highest income tax rates permanent. Since 2012, California's highest earners have paid 10.3%, 11.3% or 12.3% on the top slices of their income, rates that voters approved as Proposition 30 and extended as Proposition 55. Today those rates start at about $371,000 of taxable income for single filers and about $743,000 for joint filers. Those rates run through the 2030 tax year and then fall back to 9.3%. Prop 3, an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/) placed on the ballot by petition, deletes the end date; one of its two proponents is the president of the California Teachers Association. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it leads in both public polls: 58% to 40% in PPIC's September survey and 54% to 34% in UC Berkeley's.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The stakes are large and lopsided. The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates Prop 3 keeps $5 billion to $15 billion a year in the state budget, collected from the top 2% of taxpayers, who already pay about half of all state income taxes. Supporters frame a yes vote as no tax increase at all; opponents frame it as the "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." Both descriptions refer to the same rates. This explainer sets out what the text changes, what the rates mean in dollars, where the money goes (the 89% school figure and the LAO's 40% figure are both right, and measure different things), and who is paying for each side.
Proposition 3 deletes the 2030 end date from the Prop 30 tax rates
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends one section of the Constitution, Article XIII, section 36, which is where Prop 30 put the rates in 2012. The edits are deletions of dates:
In the two paragraphs that set the higher rates, the words "and before January 1, 2031" are struck, so the rates apply "for any taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2012" with no end.
The line in each paragraph that says it "shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031" is struck.
In the rules for the Education Protection Account, the fund that receives the money, end years such as "2030" and "2030–31" become "thereafter."
The rates themselves are unchanged. In the Constitution they are written in 2012 dollars: 10.3% on single-filer income over $250,000, 11.3% over $300,000 and 12.3% over $500,000, with parallel brackets for heads of household, all "recomputed" each year for inflation under the state's normal indexing. The Franchise Tax Board's 2025 rate schedules (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-540-tax-rate-schedules.pdf) put those thresholds at $371,479, $445,771 and $742,953 for single filers; $742,958, $891,542 and $1,485,906 for joint filers; and $505,208, $606,251 and $1,010,417 for heads of household. Prop 3 does not touch the separate 1% tax on taxable income above $1 million that voters added for mental health services, now called the Behavioral Health Services Tax. Together the two make California's top marginal rate 13.3% today. If Prop 3 fails, the top rate in 2031 would be 10.3%.
The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure "that affects the tax rates for personal income" is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is void. The LAO's notes on potential interactions for Props 40, 41 and 42, the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) and its two countermeasures, do not mention Prop 3.
California income tax rates for top earners are holding at 10.3% to 12.3% under Proposition 3 rather than falling to 9.3% after 2030, with the yearly difference shown at incomes from $400,000 to $5 million in 2026. California income tax rates in dollars: $285 at $400,000, $134,398 at $5 million
The higher rates apply only to the slices of income above each threshold, so their effect starts small and grows quickly. Using the 2025 brackets, we calculated what the Prop 30 rates add to a year's state income tax compared with taxing the same income at 9.3% above the 9.3% threshold. A single filer with $400,000 of taxable income pays $285 more. At $500,000 the difference is $1,828; at $1 million, $14,398; at $5 million, $134,398. Joint filers' brackets are twice as wide: a couple with $500,000 pays nothing extra and a couple with $1 million pays $3,655 more, rising to $28,796 at $2 million and $118,796 at $5 million. These are illustrations at 2025 brackets; by 2031 the thresholds will be higher after inflation indexing.

The "millionaire tax" is back on the California ballot: Proposition 3 would make the 2012 tax rates permanent
Proposition 3 would keep California's top income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% after 2030 instead of letting them drop to 9.3%. The brackets, what it means at $500,000 or $5 million, where the $5 billion to $15 billion goes, and who is paying for the campaign.

California's high-earner income tax is funding schools and community colleges under Proposition 3, which asks voters in November 2026 to make the 2012 rates permanent.
Proposition 3 would make California's highest income tax rates permanent. Since 2012, California's highest earners have paid 10.3%, 11.3% or 12.3% on the top slices of their income, rates that voters approved as Proposition 30 and extended as Proposition 55. Today those rates start at about $371,000 of taxable income for single filers and about $743,000 for joint filers. Those rates run through the 2030 tax year and then fall back to 9.3%. Prop 3, an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/) placed on the ballot by petition, deletes the end date; one of its two proponents is the president of the California Teachers Association. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it leads in both public polls: 58% to 40% in PPIC's September survey and 54% to 34% in UC Berkeley's.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The stakes are large and lopsided. The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates Prop 3 keeps $5 billion to $15 billion a year in the state budget, collected from the top 2% of taxpayers, who already pay about half of all state income taxes. Supporters frame a yes vote as no tax increase at all; opponents frame it as the "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." Both descriptions refer to the same rates. This explainer sets out what the text changes, what the rates mean in dollars, where the money goes (the 89% school figure and the LAO's 40% figure are both right, and measure different things), and who is paying for each side.
Proposition 3 deletes the 2030 end date from the Prop 30 tax rates
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends one section of the Constitution, Article XIII, section 36, which is where Prop 30 put the rates in 2012. The edits are deletions of dates:
In the two paragraphs that set the higher rates, the words "and before January 1, 2031" are struck, so the rates apply "for any taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2012" with no end.
The line in each paragraph that says it "shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031" is struck.
In the rules for the Education Protection Account, the fund that receives the money, end years such as "2030" and "2030–31" become "thereafter."
The rates themselves are unchanged. In the Constitution they are written in 2012 dollars: 10.3% on single-filer income over $250,000, 11.3% over $300,000 and 12.3% over $500,000, with parallel brackets for heads of household, all "recomputed" each year for inflation under the state's normal indexing. The Franchise Tax Board's 2025 rate schedules (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-540-tax-rate-schedules.pdf) put those thresholds at $371,479, $445,771 and $742,953 for single filers; $742,958, $891,542 and $1,485,906 for joint filers; and $505,208, $606,251 and $1,010,417 for heads of household. Prop 3 does not touch the separate 1% tax on taxable income above $1 million that voters added for mental health services, now called the Behavioral Health Services Tax. Together the two make California's top marginal rate 13.3% today. If Prop 3 fails, the top rate in 2031 would be 10.3%.
The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure "that affects the tax rates for personal income" is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is void. The LAO's notes on potential interactions for Props 40, 41 and 42, the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) and its two countermeasures, do not mention Prop 3.
California income tax rates for top earners are holding at 10.3% to 12.3% under Proposition 3 rather than falling to 9.3% after 2030, with the yearly difference shown at incomes from $400,000 to $5 million in 2026. California income tax rates in dollars: $285 at $400,000, $134,398 at $5 million
The higher rates apply only to the slices of income above each threshold, so their effect starts small and grows quickly. Using the 2025 brackets, we calculated what the Prop 30 rates add to a year's state income tax compared with taxing the same income at 9.3% above the 9.3% threshold. A single filer with $400,000 of taxable income pays $285 more. At $500,000 the difference is $1,828; at $1 million, $14,398; at $5 million, $134,398. Joint filers' brackets are twice as wide: a couple with $500,000 pays nothing extra and a couple with $1 million pays $3,655 more, rising to $28,796 at $2 million and $118,796 at $5 million. These are illustrations at 2025 brackets; by 2031 the thresholds will be higher after inflation indexing.

(https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But there is another ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens that is getting far less attention — and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
The basics
Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) would make an expiring state income tax on high earners permanent.
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.

California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved. The state could expect to lose $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

The basics
Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) would make an expiring state income tax on high earners permanent.
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.

Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved. Good — this is a genuinely contested empirical question. Rauh/Shyu find meaningful behavioral erosion (~45-56% of expected windfall revenue eroded in first years, and 0.8pp increase in departure rate for the top bracket), while Varner/Young/Prohofsky find little migration response. Note that even if revenue eroded 45-56%, the tax still raised substantial revenue ($104B+ cumulative per proponents; Controller's tracking site). So the behavioral response reduces but doesn't eliminate revenue. And notably, the "erosion" estimate means the state collects roughly half of the static estimate — which is still $5-10B/yr.

Also important: LAO's estimates of $5-15B presumably account for some behavioral response? Not necessarily.

Now, the state's fiscal situation: LAO projects structural deficits of $20-35 billion annually starting 2027-28. In that context, letting $5-15B of revenue lapse in 2031 would deepen the structural gap; alternatively, a "no" vote gives the Legislature pressure to reform spending. Note that the LAO says the problem is structural — spending growth outstrips revenue growth — and even with record PIT revenues there are deficits. Hmm, that's an argument that Prop 3 alone doesn't solve the structural problem, but it doesn't follow that losing $10B/year would help.

One important nuance: Because of Prop 98 and Prop 2 (2014), revenue increases get largely offset by constitutionally required spending on schools and reserves — LAO noted "constitutional spending requirements under Proposition 98 and Proposition 2 almost entirely offset revenue gains." So a "yes" vote keeps $5-15B, but roughly 40%+ goes to schools automatically, ~some to reserves, and the rest to other programs. If the tax expires, Prop 98 minimum would decline correspondingly, meaning schools would absorb ~40% of the loss through the formula, so the hit to the rest of the budget would be ~60% of the loss. Still large.

Let me consider the strongest arguments:

Yes case:
- The state faces a structural deficit; losing $5-15B/yr (about 4-6% of General Fund) starting in 2031 would force deep cuts to education, healthcare, and other services, or new broad-based taxes. Given federal Medicaid cuts (H.R. 1) hitting California (estimated $30B/yr loss to Medi-Cal per SFGate), the fiscal need is acute.
- The tax is highly progressive, hitting only top 2%, who pay about half of income tax. Empirical evidence on migration is mixed but the tax has been in place 14 years without an exodus; PPIC finds those leaving CA are less affluent than those moving in; CBPP finds state taxes have minimal impact on interstate moves.
- No new tax: rates stay as they've been since 2013. Voting no means a tax cut for the top 2% of ~$10B/yr that the state cannot afford.
- Accountability: EPA dedicated 89/11 to K-12/CCC, no admin costs, audits.
- Broad coalition support (CTA, PTA, CMA, nurses, firefighters, CA Democratic Party); most major editorial boards in favor; polls 54-58% yes.

No case:
- Permanence eliminates voter/legislative leverage; temporary taxes force periodic reevaluation. There's no urgency since expiration is 2031; a decision could be deferred to 2028/2030 (and if it fails now, proponents can re-qualify).
- Deepens reliance on the most volatile revenue source at a moment when LAO warns of a stock-market bubble and structural deficits; permanence reduces budget flexibility.
- California's top rate 13.3% is the highest in the nation; combined with federal and other taxes it's near the top globally; evidence (Rauh/Shyu) of behavioral erosion, which is a real cost, plus risk of accelerating out-migration of high earners and entrepreneurs, especially given Prop 40's chilling effect and other states (Texas, Florida, Nevada, Washington) recruiting businesses.
- Small business pass-through income is affected (S-corps, partnerships), raising costs for businesses and consumers.
- Spending per pupil is at a record high ($27,418) while outcomes remain mediocre; enrollment declining ~500k students; no reforms attached to the money. Locking in funding without accountability for results (SDUT argument).
- The initiative's rigid dedication reduces the Legislature's flexibility, and the conflict clause adds legal uncertainty interacting with Props 40/41/42.

How to weigh? Consider a median-voter/public-interest framework. Key considerations:

1. Is the revenue needed? Almost certainly yes given structural deficits and federal cuts. But "no" doesn't automatically mean revenue disappears — it could be re-authorized in 2028 or 2030. However, waiting creates uncertainty for school budgeting and would likely trigger preemptive cuts before 2031. Also, history shows extension measures passed comfortably in 2016 (63%). So the practical difference between yes now and yes in 2030 is mostly about timing certainty and the political capital spent.

2. Is permanence bad? Per se, permanence of a well-functioning, highly progressive tax that has not caused a measurable exodus is not obviously harmful. However, budget scholars (LAO) have long criticized ballot-box budgeting and rigid dedications. But Prop 3's dedication is essentially the same mechanism as Prop 30's, already in place.

3. Volatility: A real concern, but Prop 3 does route excess to reserves; and the alternative (expiry) doesn't reduce volatility of the remaining tax base — California's PIT concentration exists regardless. Actually, allowing rates to revert to 9.3% would reduce revenue concentration somewhat but not much.

4. Equity/economic efficiency: The tax burden falls on high earners and capital gains. Efficiency costs (behavioral response) exist but are modest relative to the revenue raised, and the revenue funds education — which has high social returns, especially for low-income students (LCFF). Education spending increases have been shown to improve outcomes (Jackson et al.), though California's outcomes remain weak.

5. The "tax flight" argument: mixed evidence; but the Rauh findings, even if true, imply revenue erosion not revenue loss; and CA's top earners' departure rate ~2% vs 1.5% baseline is small. Also, note that under Prop 3 rates don't change, so no new marginal incentive to leave relative to today; only relative to a counterfactual where rates drop to 9.3%. So a "no" vote could bring some high earners back/keep them, generating some economic benefit, but also forfeit $5-15B in revenue.

6. Also important: the political economy. If Prop 3 fails, will the Legislature replace the revenue with a broader, more stable tax (e.g., expanding sales tax to services)? Probably not; more likely deep cuts. Given LAO projects $20-35B structural deficits already, a further $10B revenue loss would likely be addressed with cuts to schools, healthcare, and other programs — harming lower-income Californians most. Meanwhile, beneficiaries of the tax cut are the top 2%.

Weighing the distributional and practical considerations: the measure preserves revenue that funds schools and healthcare, affects only the top 2%, changes no one's taxes relative to current law, and has strong institutional support. Opposition arguments are largely about principle (temporary means temporary), spending reform, and contested migration evidence, plus the loss of budget flexibility.

Counter-consideration: is the state's problem one of revenue or spending? LAO says structural: spending growth outstrips revenue growth. Adding permanent revenue doesn't fix the structural gap but it does reduce it (in 2031, revenue would drop). Actually if you reject Prop 3, revenue drops $5-15B in 2031 while Prop 98 spending requirements also drop ~40%, so the structural gap widens by roughly 60% of the loss — deepening deficits.

Hmm, but there's another angle: the LAO notes that revenue increases get "almost entirely offset" by Prop 98 and Prop 2 requirements — meaning the state's discretionary gain from new revenue is small. Conversely, losing revenue reduces required school spending automatically, so the discretionary hit is smaller than headline. Let me quantify: LAO says roughly 40% goes to schools/community colleges, some to reserves, rest to other programs. If the tax expires, the Prop 98 guarantee falls by roughly the school share, meaning schools would see reduced funding through the formula but the state's non-Prop 98 budget would lose ~60% ($3-9B) — still substantial.

Also note that in 2031, when it expires, the LAO says the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements (SPUR's phrasing) — over time Prop 98 minimum could decline.

I think the balance tips toward "yes," mainly because:
- The measure imposes no new tax and no rate increase relative to current law; it prevents a ~$10B/yr revenue loss concentrated as a tax cut for the top 2% at a time when the state faces structural deficits and federal Medicaid cuts.
- Empirical evidence on migration is mixed, and the burden of proof for a large economic harm is not met; PPIC/CBPP evidence and California's actual experience (14 years, $104-119B raised, high-earner out-migration low relative to other states) suggest the harm is modest.
- The revenue supports education and children's healthcare with meaningful accountability provisions.

But let me check a couple more things to be fair and thorough:
1. Is there any credible nonpartisan group opposing on grounds other than ideology (e.g., Bay Area Council, California Chamber of Commerce, PPIC)? Chamber of Commerce? Let me check who's on the no side beyond taxpayer groups: California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association, Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, Howard Jarvis, Reform California. Also possibly some Democrats/moderate business groups? The LA Times said Prop 3 "garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Prop 40" — interesting, so some wealthy interests support Prop 3 as an alternative to Prop 40 (maybe to demonstrate revenue can be raised without a wealth tax; or because of the conflict clause).

2. Check whether there's a concern that Prop 3's conflict clause could nullify Prop 41/42 (which some voters might want). If Prop 3 gets more yes votes than Prop 41 or 42 and they're deemed conflicting (affecting "tax rates for personal income"), Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is null and void. Prop 41 concerns special taxes and Gann limit exemptions; Prop 42 concerns taxes on personal property. Arguably neither "affects the tax rates for personal income," though tax professors suggested Prop 42 could be read to nullify Prop 3 (a conflict). Under the constitutional rule, whichever gets more votes prevails. Prop 3 polls higher (54-58%) than 41/42 (~50%), so Prop 3 would likely prevail — meaning the Prop 3 clause could theoretically void Prop 41/42 entirely ("in their entirety"), which would be a consequential, possibly unintended effect: it would also remove Prop 41/42's nullification of Prop 40... hmm, actually if Prop 41/42 were void, then Prop 40 (if passed) would take effect. Interesting but speculative. Courts would decide. This is a real "hidden risk" consideration: voting yes on Prop 3 might inadvertently affect the billionaire-tax countermeasures. But that's speculative and probably minor; also many would see it as fine.

Let me quickly check the LA Times last-minute guide and the californiatoday guide for further "what's easy to miss" items about Prop 3, and see if any consumer-protection angle (e.g., whether Prop 3 contains a poison pill or unusual provisions like the proponent standing clause). Also check the SF Chronicle editorial for the yes case and whether it acknowledges downsides.

The "millionaire tax" is back on the California ballot: Proposition 3 would make the 2012 tax rates permanent
Proposition 3 would keep California's top income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% after 2030 instead of letting them drop to 9.3%. The brackets, what it means at $500,000 or $5 million, where the $5 billion to $15 billion goes, and who is paying for the campaign.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 15, 2026

California's high-earner income tax is funding schools and community colleges under Proposition 3, which asks voters in November 2026 to make the 2012 rates permanent.
Proposition 3 would make California's highest income tax rates permanent. Since 2012, California's highest earners have paid 10.3%, 11.3% or 12.3% on the top slices of their income, rates that voters approved as Proposition 30 and extended as Proposition 55. Today those rates start at about $371,000 of taxable income for single filers and about $743,000 for joint filers. Those rates run through the 2030 tax year and then fall back to 9.3%. Prop 3, an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/) placed on the ballot by petition, deletes the end date; one of its two proponents is the president of the California Teachers Association. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it leads in both public polls: 58% to 40% in PPIC's September survey and 54% to 34% in UC Berkeley's.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The stakes are large and lopsided. The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates Prop 3 keeps $5 billion to $15 billion a year in the state budget, collected from the top 2% of taxpayers, who already pay about half of all state income taxes. Supporters frame a yes vote as no tax increase at all; opponents frame it as the "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." Both descriptions refer to the same rates. This explainer sets out what the text changes, what the rates mean in dollars, where the money goes (the 89% school figure and the LAO's 40% figure are both right, and measure different things), and who is paying for each side.
Proposition 3 deletes the 2030 end date from the Prop 30 tax rates
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends one section of the Constitution, Article XIII, section 36, which is where Prop 30 put the rates in 2012. The edits are deletions of dates:
In the two paragraphs that set the higher rates, the words "and before January 1, 2031" are struck, so the rates apply "for any taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2012" with no end.
The line in each paragraph that says it "shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031" is struck.
In the rules for the Education Protection Account, the fund that receives the money, end years such as "2030" and "2030–31" become "thereafter."
The rates themselves are unchanged. In the Constitution they are written in 2012 dollars: 10.3% on single-filer income over $250,000, 11.3% over $300,000 and 12.3% over $500,000, with parallel brackets for heads of household, all "recomputed" each year for inflation under the state's normal indexing. The Franchise Tax Board's 2025 rate schedules (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-540-tax-rate-schedules.pdf) put those thresholds at $371,479, $445,771 and $742,953 for single filers; $742,958, $891,542 and $1,485,906 for joint filers; and $505,208, $606,251 and $1,010,417 for heads of household. Prop 3 does not touch the separate 1% tax on taxable income above $1 million that voters added for mental health services, now called the Behavioral Health Services Tax. Together the two make California's top marginal rate 13.3% today. If Prop 3 fails, the top rate in 2031 would be 10.3%.
The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure "that affects the tax rates for personal income" is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is void. The LAO's notes on potential interactions for Props 40, 41 and 42, the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) and its two countermeasures, do not mention Prop 3.
California income tax rates for top earners are holding at 10.3% to 12.3% under Proposition 3 rather than falling to 9.3% after 2030, with the yearly difference shown at incomes from $400,000 to $5 million in 2026. California income tax rates in dollars: $285 at $400,000, $134,398 at $5 million
The higher rates apply only to the slices of income above each threshold, so their effect starts small and grows quickly. Using the 2025 brackets, we calculated what the Prop 30 rates add to a year's state income tax compared with taxing the same income at 9.3% above the 9.3% threshold. A single filer with $400,000 of taxable income pays $285 more. At $500,000 the difference is $1,828; at $1 million, $14,398; at $5 million, $134,398. Joint filers' brackets are twice as wide: a couple with $500,000 pays nothing extra and a couple with $1 million pays $3,655 more, rising to $28,796 at $2 million and $118,796 at $5 million. These are illustrations at 2025 brackets; by 2031 the thresholds will be higher after inflation indexing.

The basics
Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) would make an expiring state income tax on high earners permanent.
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.

Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved. The state could expect to lose $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

content.text:
"pay about half of all state income taxes." Because much of their income comes from investments and capital gains, the yield swings with the stock market: "In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion." The state plans about $250 billion in General Fund spending this year, according to the same analysis; our 2026–27 state budget guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/legal/2026-27-california-state-budget-guide/) covers where it goes.
Prop 3's school money: 89% to K–12 schools, and about 40% of the total in practice
Two official figures about where Prop 3's money goes look contradictory and are both accurate. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm) says the measure "allocates tax revenues 89% to K–12 schools, 11% to community colleges." The LAO says "roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges" and "the rest would go to other state programs," with part set aside in reserves.
The first figure describes the Education Protection Account. Section 36 sends the revenue there and splits it 89% to school districts, county offices and charter schools and 11% to community college districts, as general-purpose money that local boards spend "in open session" and may not use "for salaries or benefits of administrators or any other administrative costs." Each district must publish an annual accounting online, the account is audited, and the Attorney General or a district attorney can seek "civil or criminal penalties" for misuse.
The second figure describes the net effect on the budget. The same section deems the account's revenue "General Fund revenues" for Proposition 98, the constitutional minimum for school and community college funding. The account's money therefore counts toward that minimum rather than adding on top of it, and the state's other spending on schools adjusts around it. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0016%29.pdf) to the Attorney General puts the result at "typically, about 40 percent." The measure's own findings say as much: the revenue goes to schools, and "State funding is freed up to help balance the budget and provide for a Rainy Day Fund."
Prop 30 in 2012, Prop 55 in 2016, Prop 3 in 2026
Prop 30 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2012 with 7,014,114 votes, 55.4%; it also raised the state sales tax by a quarter cent from 2013 through 2016. Prop 55 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2016 with 8,594,273 votes, 63.3%, extending the income tax rates, but not the sales tax, through 2030. Prop 3 would be the third vote on the same rates and the first without an expiration date. Its findings say the tax "has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other essential services" and that letting it expire "would result in an immediate reduction to state revenues of over $10 billion"; those are the proponents' figures.
Proposition 3's backers and the $46 million campaign
The proponents of record are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, according to the Attorney General's active-measures list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) (file 25-0016, title and summary issued November 4, 2025). Goldberg signs the ballot argument as president of the California Teachers Association.
The money is almost entirely on one side. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) for Prop 3 reports $46,260,006 contributed in support through October 6, across four committees, and $5,500 in opposition, to a committee sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association. The FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 12, puts support from top contributors at $49.7 million. The main Yes committee's largest donors are the California Teachers Association's issues committee ($33.4 million), the National Education Association ($7.5 million), the California School Employees Association ($2.6 million), the California Federation of Teachers ($1.75 million) and SEIU California ($1.5 million). No opposing committee has reached the list's $1 million threshold.
The arguments: "Not a new tax" versus "temporary" taxes made permanent
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Goldberg, California School Nurses Organization president Katie Nilsson and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California president Jodi Hicks, says "Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone" and that without it "millionaires and billionaires" would get "a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities." It says the 8 million public school and community college students "face billions in cuts" without the revenue, and stresses that the money cannot be spent "on bureaucracy or administrative overhead," which the text supports for the Education Protection Account itself.
The No argument, signed by the presidents of the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says "Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary" and that Prop 3 turns them into "PERMANENTLY higher income taxes." It argues that Californians already pay "the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes," that the state "turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years," and that "California doesn't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem." The rebuttal, led by Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association president Jon Coupal, calls the measure "the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." The deficit and spending figures are the campaign's; all ballot arguments carry the guide's note that they "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 3
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters found 58% yes, 40% no and 2% undecided. The split is partisan: Democrats 82% to 16% in favor, Republicans 18% to 80% against, independents 57% to 41% in favor. Voters in households earning $100,000 or more backed it 55% to 43%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 17% named Prop 3. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf), fielded September 15–20, found 54% yes, 34% no and 13% undecided, a "solid 20-point lead," in contrast with the 45–42 split it found on the Prop 40 billionaire tax.
The California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 3 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The supporters listed in the Voter Information Guide are the California Teachers Association, the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California; the opponents listed are the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Proposition 3 after November 3: Permanent rates from 2031, or a return to 9.3%
If Prop 3 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11, but nothing changes on anyone's tax bill: the same rates continue, and the difference first shows up in the 2031 tax year, when they would otherwise have ended. Because the rates would sit in the Constitution, changing them would take another statewide vote. If it fails, the rates still apply through the 2030 tax year, and from 2031 the top rate on income below $1 million becomes 9.3%, and the state budget would lose an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion a year.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, FTB 2025 rate schedules, campaign-finance data as of October 12, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party and governor positions as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 20, 2026.

Story Title:
Teachers unions make pitch to renew California tax worth billions for education
September 29, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Vicky-Chon-canvassing-091926-scaled.jpeg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Top Takeaways
A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. Barrera, an ally of organized labor, is the president of the San Diego Unified school board and is running for state superintendent of public instruction.
To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.
Chon and the 68 other Fremont Unified teachers knocked on 2,533 doors as part of the California Teachers Association’s Sept. 19 day of action for Prop. 3; 1,150 teachers from 69 districts elsewhere in the state knocked on 36,509 doors. Combined, they set a one-day canvassing record, CTA said.
WATCH: Fremont teachers union President Vicky Chon explains why she’s canvassing for Proposition 3.
Teachers are the first prong of the Yes on 3 campaign’s two-prong strategy. The other involves raising and spending money. Lots of it.
In the Sept. 24 filing to the California Secretary of State, the Yes on 3 campaign had raised $46.8 million, not counting donations under $1,000. The No on 3 campaign has raised $5,500 in total. The Family Business Association of California PAC gave $5,000 of the total.
The Yes campaign has raised $8,509 for every $1 of opposition dollars.
CTA, which led the signature drive to put Prop. 3 on the ballot, contributed $33.3 million – 71% of the total – while the CTA’s parent union, the National Education Association, donated $10 million. The California Federation of Teachers, the smaller of two California teachers unions, gave $1.75 million to go with the Service Employees International Union’s (SEIU) $1.5 million.
CTA’s elected 700-delegate State Council allocated the money in June, “not taking anything for granted,” said CTA President David Goldberg. CTA was less worried about the opposition than with the sheer number of 14 initiatives on the ballot. It’s been more important to raise awareness of Prop. 3 “above the noise,” he said.
Now, with five weeks to go before the election, he said, “I would assume there is enough for every scenario to win this,” including TV ads. ”It’s definitely an option.”
Two choices: a wealth tax and/or an income tax?
Prop. 3 is one of two tax-raising initiatives on the November ballot. The other, far more contentious one, is Prop. 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)), which would create the nation’s first tax on the net worth of the state’s 200-plus billionaires.
The independent, nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the one-time, 5% tax on most of the billionaires’ assets would yield tens of billions of dollars. But it also cautioned it could result in a loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue if the richest of the rich follow the lead of Elon Musk and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin and move out of state to cheaper tax states like Florida and Texas.
CTA opposes Prop. 40 because TK-12 and community colleges would receive only 10% of the take from Prop. 40, a smaller ratio than the 40% that they already get annually as their share of the state’s general fund revenue under a constitutional amendment passed in 1988.
Prop. 3 would continue that ratio. The LAO projects that, depending on volatile income and capital tax revenue, Prop. 3 would continue to bring in $5 billion to $15 billion to the general fund with 40% – $2 billion to $6 billion – going to schools and community colleges annually.
A Prop. 3 surcharge of 1% starts with taxable income of $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers. It would jump to an additional 3 percentage points for those single filers making more than $743,000 or $1.5 million for joint filers.
More than 50% support in a new voter survey
Conventional thinking of pollsters and veteran political observers is that multiple tax measures on the same ballot, especially complex initiatives like the wealth tax, could hurt the chances of all tax initiatives: Frustrated voters would throw up their hands and vote “no” across their ballots.
But, based on the Sept. 25 voter survey by the UC Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies, that doesn’t seem to be happening; voters appear to be heading in opposite directions in support for Prop. 3 and Prop. 40.
Compared with a prior survey in August, support for Prop. 3 rose to 54% in favor, 34% opposed, and 13% undecided.
Support for Prop. 40 had fallen from above 50% in August to 45% in favor, 42% against, and 13% undecided, amid an onslaught of anti-Prop. 40 TV ads.
Although Fremont offers a small sample size — Democrats outnumber Republicans three to one in the Alameda County city — canvassing teachers said they heard widespread support for Prop. 3.
Nicole Black, a veteran kindergarten teacher, said someone came to the door in about half of the 50 houses she visited, with 20 of those indicating support, some asking for more information, and no one outright saying no. William Jung, a high school teacher, reported fewer conversations but proportionally higher support.
Vicky Chon encountered only one no – a shirtless man working in his garage who dismissed her with a flip of the hand, saying, “No more taxes.” But a woman who had said through her Ring doorbell video camera that she was driving her father to an appointment later was working in her garden and said she was all in. And an elderly lady with patchy English said, yes, she would vote for it, too.
No one wanted more details of Prop. 3 or asked about the wealth tax, so Chon and colleagues didn’t have to bring it up. They could stay on message: Prop. 3 will continue an existing tax. Voting yes will keep the status quo and prevent future layoffs of teachers.
In the coming weeks, voters can expect to be inundated with tens of millions of dollars worth of ads for, but mainly against, Prop. 40. Opponents have already spent $87 million – 85% of the $219 million total (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) – compared with $32 million by the proponents.
Meanwhile, teachers will be going door to door every weekend, Goldberg said. “We always knew a lot would rest on our shoulders,” he said. “No other organization can match our capacity in every community.”

Because much of their income comes from investments and capital gains, the yield swings with the stock market: "In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion." The state plans about $250 billion in General Fund spending this year, according to the same analysis; our 2026–27 state budget guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/legal/2026-27-california-state-budget-guide/) covers where it goes.
Prop 3's school money: 89% to K–12 schools, and about 40% of the total in practice
Two official figures about where Prop 3's money goes look contradictory and are both accurate. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm) says the measure "allocates tax revenues 89% to K–12 schools, 11% to community colleges." The LAO says "roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges" and "the rest would go to other state programs," with part set aside in reserves.
The first figure describes the Education Protection Account. Section 36 sends the revenue there and splits it 89% to school districts, county offices and charter schools and 11% to community college districts, as general-purpose money that local boards spend "in open session" and may not use "for salaries or benefits of administrators or any other administrative costs." Each district must publish an annual accounting online, the account is audited, and the Attorney General or a district attorney can seek "civil or criminal penalties" for misuse.
The second figure describes the net effect on the budget. The same section deems the account's revenue "General Fund revenues" for Proposition 98, the constitutional minimum for school and community college funding. The account's money therefore counts toward that minimum rather than adding on top of it, and the state's other spending on schools adjusts around it. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0016%29.pdf) to the Attorney General puts the result at "typically, about 40 percent." The measure's own findings say as much: the revenue goes to schools, and "State funding is freed up to help balance the budget and provide for a Rainy Day Fund."
Prop 30 in 2012, Prop 55 in 2016, Prop 3 in 2026
Prop 30 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2012 with 7,014,114 votes, 55.4%; it also raised the state sales tax by a quarter cent from 2013 through 2016. Prop 55 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2016 with 8,594,273 votes, 63.3%, extending the income tax rates, but not the sales tax, through 2030. Prop 3 would be the third vote on the same rates and the first without an expiration date. Its findings say the tax "has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other essential services" and that letting it expire "would result in an immediate reduction to state revenues of over $10 billion"; those are the proponents' figures.
Proposition 3's backers and the $46 million campaign
The proponents of record are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, according to the Attorney General's active-measures list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) (file 25-0016, title and summary issued November 4, 2025). Goldberg signs the ballot argument as president of the California Teachers Association.
The money is almost entirely on one side. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) for Prop 3 reports $46,260,006 contributed in support through October 6, across four committees, and $5,500 in opposition, to a committee sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association. The FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 12, puts support from top contributors at $49.7 million. The main Yes committee's largest donors are the California Teachers Association's issues committee ($33.4 million), the National Education Association ($7.5 million), the California School Employees Association ($2.6 million), the California Federation of Teachers ($1.75 million) and SEIU California ($1.5 million). No opposing committee has reached the list's $1 million threshold.
The arguments: "Not a new tax" versus "temporary" taxes made permanent
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Goldberg, California School Nurses Organization president Katie Nilsson and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California president Jodi Hicks, says "Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone" and that without it "millionaires and billionaires" would get "a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities." It says the 8 million public school and community college students "face billions in cuts" without the revenue, and stresses that the money cannot be spent "on bureaucracy or administrative overhead," which the text supports for the Education Protection Account itself.
The No argument, signed by the presidents of the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says "Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary" and that Prop 3 turns them into "PERMANENTLY higher income taxes." It argues that Californians already pay "the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes," that the state "turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years," and that "California doesn't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem." The rebuttal, led by Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association president Jon Coupal, calls the measure "the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." The deficit and spending figures are the campaign's; all ballot arguments carry the guide's note that they "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 3
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters found 58% yes, 40% no and 2% undecided. The split is partisan: Democrats 82% to 16% in favor, Republicans 18% to 80% against, independents 57% to 41% in favor. Voters in households earning $100,000 or more backed it 55% to 43%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 17% named Prop 3. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf), fielded September 15–20, found 54% yes, 34% no and 13% undecided, a "solid 20-point lead," in contrast with the 45–42 split it found on the Prop 40 billionaire tax.
The California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 3 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The supporters listed in the Voter Information Guide are the California Teachers Association, the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California; the opponents listed are the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Proposition 3 after November 3: Permanent rates from 2031, or a return to 9.3%
If Prop 3 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11, but nothing changes on anyone's tax bill: the same rates continue, and the difference first shows up in the 2031 tax year, when they would otherwise have ended. Because the rates would sit in the Constitution, changing them would take another statewide vote. If it fails, the rates still apply through the 2030 tax year, and from 2031 the top rate on income below $1 million becomes 9.3%, and the state budget would lose an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion a year.

Polling and endorsements on Proposition 3
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters found 58% yes, 40% no and 2% undecided. The split is partisan: Democrats 82% to 16% in favor, Republicans 18% to 80% against, independents 57% to 41% in favor. Voters in households earning $100,000 or more backed it 55% to 43%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 17% named Prop 3. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf), fielded September 15–20, found 54% yes, 34% no and 13% undecided, a "solid 20-point lead," in contrast with the 45–42 split it found on the Prop 40 billionaire tax.
The California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 3 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The supporters listed in the Voter Information Guide are the California Teachers Association, the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California; the opponents listed are the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Proposition 3 after November 3: Permanent rates from 2031, or a return to 9.3%
If Prop 3 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11, but nothing changes on anyone's tax bill: the same rates continue, and the difference first shows up in the 2031 tax year, when they would otherwise have ended. Because the rates would sit in the Constitution, changing them would take another statewide vote. If it fails, the rates still apply through the 2030 tax year, and from 2031 the top rate on income below $1 million becomes 9.3%, and the state budget would lose an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion a year.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, FTB 2025 rate schedules, campaign-finance data as of October 12, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party and governor positions as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 20, 2026.
