Story Title:
Teachers unions make pitch to renew California tax worth billions for education
September 29, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Vicky-Chon-canvassing-091926-scaled.jpeg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Top Takeaways
A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. Barrera, an ally of organized labor, is the president of the San Diego Unified school board and is running for state superintendent of public instruction.
To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.
Chon and the 68 other Fremont Unified teachers knocked on 2,533 doors as part of the California Teachers Association’s Sept. 19 day of action for Prop. 3; 1,150 teachers from 69 districts elsewhere in the state knocked on 36,509 doors. Combined, they set a one-day canvassing record, CTA said.
WATCH: Fremont teachers union President Vicky Chon explains why she’s canvassing for Proposition 3.
Teachers are the first prong of the Yes on 3 campaign’s two-prong strategy. The other involves raising and spending money. Lots of it.
In the Sept. 24 filing to the California Secretary of State, the Yes on 3 campaign had raised $46.8 million, not counting donations under $1,000. The No on 3 campaign has raised $5,500 in total. The Family Business Association of California PAC gave $5,000 of the total.
The Yes campaign has raised $8,509 for every $1 of opposition dollars.
CTA, which led the signature drive to put Prop. 3 on the ballot, contributed $33.3 million – 71% of the total – while the CTA’s parent union, the National Education Association, donated $10 million. The California Federation of Teachers, the smaller of two California teachers unions, gave $1.75 million to go with the Service Employees International Union’s (SEIU) $1.5 million.
CTA’s elected 700-delegate State Council allocated the money in June, “not taking anything for granted,” said CTA President David Goldberg. CTA was less worried about the opposition than with the sheer number of 14 initiatives on the ballot. It’s been more important to raise awareness of Prop. 3 “above the noise,” he said.
Now, with five weeks to go before the election, he said, “I would assume there is enough for every scenario to win this,” including TV ads. ”It’s definitely an option.”
Two choices: a wealth tax and/or an income tax?
Prop. 3 is one of two tax-raising initiatives on the November ballot. The other, far more contentious one, is Prop. 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)), which would create the nation’s first tax on the net worth of the state’s 200-plus billionaires.
The independent, nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the one-time, 5% tax on most of the billionaires’ assets would yield tens of billions of dollars. But it also cautioned it could result in a loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue if the richest of the rich follow the lead of Elon Musk and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin and move out of state to cheaper tax states like Florida and Texas.
CTA opposes Prop. 40 because TK-12 and community colleges would receive only 10% of the take from Prop. 40, a smaller ratio than the 40% that they already get annually as their share of the state’s general fund revenue under a constitutional amendment passed in 1988.
Prop. 3 would continue that ratio. The LAO projects that, depending on volatile income and capital tax revenue, Prop. 3 would continue to bring in $5 billion to $15 billion to the general fund with 40% – $2 billion to $6 billion – going to schools and community colleges annually.
A Prop. 3 surcharge of 1% starts with taxable income of $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers. It would jump to an additional 3 percentage points for those single filers making more than $743,000 or $1.5 million for joint filers.
More than 50% support in a new voter survey
Conventional thinking of pollsters and veteran political observers is that multiple tax measures on the same ballot, especially complex initiatives like the wealth tax, could hurt the chances of all tax initiatives: Frustrated voters would throw up their hands and vote “no” across their ballots.
But, based on the Sept. 25 voter survey by the UC Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies, that doesn’t seem to be happening; voters appear to be heading in opposite directions in support for Prop. 3 and Prop. 40.
Compared with a prior survey in August, support for Prop. 3 rose to 54% in favor, 34% opposed, and 13% undecided.
Support for Prop. 40 had fallen from above 50% in August to 45% in favor, 42% against, and 13% undecided, amid an onslaught of anti-Prop. 40 TV ads.
Although Fremont offers a small sample size — Democrats outnumber Republicans three to one in the Alameda County city — canvassing teachers said they heard widespread support for Prop. 3.
Nicole Black, a veteran kindergarten teacher, said someone came to the door in about half of the 50 houses she visited, with 20 of those indicating support, some asking for more information, and no one outright saying no. William Jung, a high school teacher, reported fewer conversations but proportionally higher support.
Vicky Chon encountered only one no – a shirtless man working in his garage who dismissed her with a flip of the hand, saying, “No more taxes.” But a woman who had said through her Ring doorbell video camera that she was driving her father to an appointment later was working in her garden and said she was all in. And an elderly lady with patchy English said, yes, she would vote for it, too.
No one wanted more details of Prop. 3 or asked about the wealth tax, so Chon and colleagues didn’t have to bring it up. They could stay on message: Prop. 3 will continue an existing tax. Voting yes will keep the status quo and prevent future layoffs of teachers.
In the coming weeks, voters can expect to be inundated with tens of millions of dollars worth of ads for, but mainly against, Prop. 40. Opponents have already spent $87 million – 85% of the $219 million total (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) – compared with $32 million by the proponents.
Meanwhile, teachers will be going door to door every weekend, Goldberg said. “We always knew a lot would rest on our shoulders,” he said. “No other organization can match our capacity in every community.”

Story Title:
Teachers unions make pitch to renew California tax worth billions for education
September 29, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Vicky-Chon-canvassing-091926-scaled.jpeg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Top Takeaways
A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. Barrera, an ally of organized labor, is the president of the San Diego Unified school board and is running for state superintendent of public instruction.
To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.
Chon and the 68 other Fremont Unified teachers knocked on 2,533 doors as part of the California Teachers Association’s Sept. 19 day of action for Prop. 3; 1,150 teachers from 69 districts elsewhere in the state knocked on 36,509 doors. Combined, they set a one-day canvassing record, CTA said.
WATCH: Fremont teachers union President Vicky Chon explains why she’s canvassing for Proposition 3.
Teachers are the first prong of the Yes on 3 campaign’s two-prong strategy. The other involves raising and spending money. Lots of it.
In the Sept. 24 filing to the California Secretary of State, the Yes on 3 campaign had raised $46.8 million, not counting donations under $1,000. The No on 3 campaign has raised $5,500 in total. The Family Business Association of California PAC gave $5,000 of the total.
The Yes campaign has raised $8,509 for every $1 of opposition dollars.
CTA, which led the signature drive to put Prop. 3 on the ballot, contributed $33.3 million – 71% of the total – while the CTA’s parent union, the National Education Association, donated $10 million. The California Federation of Teachers, the smaller of two California teachers unions, gave $1.75 million to go with the Service Employees International Union’s (SEIU) $1.5 million.
CTA’s elected 700-delegate State Council allocated the money in June, “not taking anything for granted,” said CTA President David Goldberg. CTA was less worried about the opposition than with the sheer number of 14 initiatives on the ballot. It’s been more important to raise awareness of Prop. 3 “above the noise,” he said.
Now, with five weeks to go before the election, he said, “I would assume there is enough for every scenario to win this,” including TV ads. ”It’s definitely an option.”
Two choices: a wealth tax and/or an income tax?
Prop. 3 is one of two tax-raising initiatives on the November ballot. The other, far more contentious one, is Prop. 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)), which would create the nation’s first tax on the net worth of the state’s 200-plus billionaires.
The independent, nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the one-time, 5% tax on most of the billionaires’ assets would yield tens of billions of dollars. But it also cautioned it could result in a loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue if the richest of the rich follow the lead of Elon Musk and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin and move out of state to cheaper tax states like Florida and Texas.
CTA opposes Prop. 40 because TK-12 and community colleges would receive only 10% of the take from Prop. 40, a smaller ratio than the 40% that they already get annually as their share of the state’s general fund revenue under a constitutional amendment passed in 1988.
Prop. 3 would continue that ratio. The LAO projects that, depending on volatile income and capital tax revenue, Prop. 3 would continue to bring in $5 billion to $15 billion to the general fund with 40% – $2 billion to $6 billion – going to schools and community colleges annually.
A Prop. 3 surcharge of 1% starts with taxable income of $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers. It would jump to an additional 3 percentage points for those single filers making more than $743,000 or $1.5 million for joint filers.
More than 50% support in a new voter survey
Conventional thinking of pollsters and veteran political observers is that multiple tax measures on the same ballot, especially complex initiatives like the wealth tax, could hurt the chances of all tax initiatives: Frustrated voters would throw up their hands and vote “no” across their ballots.
But, based on the Sept. 25 voter survey by the UC Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies, that doesn’t seem to be happening; voters appear to be heading in opposite directions in support for Prop. 3 and Prop. 40.
Compared with a prior survey in August, support for Prop. 3 rose to 54% in favor, 34% opposed, and 13% undecided.
Support for Prop. 40 had fallen from above 50% in August to 45% in favor, 42% against, and 13% undecided, amid an onslaught of anti-Prop. 40 TV ads.
Although Fremont offers a small sample size — Democrats outnumber Republicans three to one in the Alameda County city — canvassing teachers said they heard widespread support for Prop. 3.
Nicole Black, a veteran kindergarten teacher, said someone came to the door in about half of the 50 houses she visited, with 20 of those indicating support, some asking for more information, and no one outright saying no. William Jung, a high school teacher, reported fewer conversations but proportionally higher support.
Vicky Chon encountered only one no – a shirtless man working in his garage who dismissed her with a flip of the hand, saying, “No more taxes.” But a woman who had said through her Ring doorbell video camera that she was driving her father to an appointment later was working in her garden and said she was all in. And an elderly lady with patchy English said, yes, she would vote for it, too.
No one wanted more details of Prop. 3 or asked about the wealth tax, so Chon and colleagues didn’t have to bring it up. They could stay on message: Prop. 3 will continue an existing tax. Voting yes will keep the status quo and prevent future layoffs of teachers.
In the coming weeks, voters can expect to be inundated with tens of millions of dollars worth of ads for, but mainly against, Prop. 40. Opponents have already spent $87 million – 85% of the $219 million total (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) – compared with $32 million by the proponents.
Meanwhile, teachers will be going door to door every weekend, Goldberg said. “We always knew a lot would rest on our shoulders,” he said. “No other organization can match our capacity in every community.”

content.text:
"pay about half of all state income taxes." Because much of their income comes from investments and capital gains, the yield swings with the stock market: "In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion." The state plans about $250 billion in General Fund spending this year, according to the same analysis; our 2026–27 state budget guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/legal/2026-27-california-state-budget-guide/) covers where it goes.
Prop 3's school money: 89% to K–12 schools, and about 40% of the total in practice
Two official figures about where Prop 3's money goes look contradictory and are both accurate. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm) says the measure "allocates tax revenues 89% to K–12 schools, 11% to community colleges." The LAO says "roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges" and "the rest would go to other state programs," with part set aside in reserves.
The first figure describes the Education Protection Account. Section 36 sends the revenue there and splits it 89% to school districts, county offices and charter schools and 11% to community college districts, as general-purpose money that local boards spend "in open session" and may not use "for salaries or benefits of administrators or any other administrative costs." Each district must publish an annual accounting online, the account is audited, and the Attorney General or a district attorney can seek "civil or criminal penalties" for misuse.
The second figure describes the net effect on the budget. The same section deems the account's revenue "General Fund revenues" for Proposition 98, the constitutional minimum for school and community college funding. The account's money therefore counts toward that minimum rather than adding on top of it, and the state's other spending on schools adjusts around it. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0016%29.pdf) to the Attorney General puts the result at "typically, about 40 percent." The measure's own findings say as much: the revenue goes to schools, and "State funding is freed up to help balance the budget and provide for a Rainy Day Fund."
Prop 30 in 2012, Prop 55 in 2016, Prop 3 in 2026
Prop 30 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2012 with 7,014,114 votes, 55.4%; it also raised the state sales tax by a quarter cent from 2013 through 2016. Prop 55 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2016 with 8,594,273 votes, 63.3%, extending the income tax rates, but not the sales tax, through 2030. Prop 3 would be the third vote on the same rates and the first without an expiration date. Its findings say the tax "has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other essential services" and that letting it expire "would result in an immediate reduction to state revenues of over $10 billion"; those are the proponents' figures.
Proposition 3's backers and the $46 million campaign
The proponents of record are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, according to the Attorney General's active-measures list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) (file 25-0016, title and summary issued November 4, 2025). Goldberg signs the ballot argument as president of the California Teachers Association.
The money is almost entirely on one side. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) for Prop 3 reports $46,260,006 contributed in support through October 6, across four committees, and $5,500 in opposition, to a committee sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association. The FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 12, puts support from top contributors at $49.7 million. The main Yes committee's largest donors are the California Teachers Association's issues committee ($33.4 million), the National Education Association ($7.5 million), the California School Employees Association ($2.6 million), the California Federation of Teachers ($1.75 million) and SEIU California ($1.5 million). No opposing committee has reached the list's $1 million threshold.
The arguments: "Not a new tax" versus "temporary" taxes made permanent
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Goldberg, California School Nurses Organization president Katie Nilsson and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California president Jodi Hicks, says "Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone" and that without it "millionaires and billionaires" would get "a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities." It says the 8 million public school and community college students "face billions in cuts" without the revenue, and stresses that the money cannot be spent "on bureaucracy or administrative overhead," which the text supports for the Education Protection Account itself.
The No argument, signed by the presidents of the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says "Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary" and that Prop 3 turns them into "PERMANENTLY higher income taxes." It argues that Californians already pay "the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes," that the state "turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years," and that "California doesn't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem." The rebuttal, led by Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association president Jon Coupal, calls the measure "the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." The deficit and spending figures are the campaign's; all ballot arguments carry the guide's note that they "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 3
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters found 58% yes, 40% no and 2% undecided. The split is partisan: Democrats 82% to 16% in favor, Republicans 18% to 80% against, independents 57% to 41% in favor. Voters in households earning $100,000 or more backed it 55% to 43%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 17% named Prop 3. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf), fielded September 15–20, found 54% yes, 34% no and 13% undecided, a "solid 20-point lead," in contrast with the 45–42 split it found on the Prop 40 billionaire tax.
The California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 3 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The supporters listed in the Voter Information Guide are the California Teachers Association, the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California; the opponents listed are the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Proposition 3 after November 3: Permanent rates from 2031, or a return to 9.3%
If Prop 3 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11, but nothing changes on anyone's tax bill: the same rates continue, and the difference first shows up in the 2031 tax year, when they would otherwise have ended. Because the rates would sit in the Constitution, changing them would take another statewide vote. If it fails, the rates still apply through the 2030 tax year, and from 2031 the top rate on income below $1 million becomes 9.3%, and the state budget would lose an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion a year.

Story Title:
Teachers unions make pitch to renew California tax worth billions for education
September 29, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Vicky-Chon-canvassing-091926-scaled.jpeg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Top Takeaways
A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. Barrera, an ally of organized labor, is the president of the San Diego Unified school board and is running for state superintendent of public instruction.
To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.
Chon and the 68 other Fremont Unified teachers knocked on 2,533 doors as part of the California Teachers Association’s Sept. 19 day of action for Prop. 3; 1,150 teachers from 69 districts elsewhere in the state knocked on 36,509 doors. Combined, they set a one-day canvassing record, CTA said.
WATCH: Fremont teachers union President Vicky Chon explains why she’s canvassing for Proposition 3.
Teachers are the first prong of the Yes on 3 campaign’s two-prong strategy. The other involves raising and spending money. Lots of it.
In the Sept. 24 filing to the California Secretary of State, the Yes on 3 campaign had raised $46.8 million, not counting donations under $1,000. The No on 3 campaign has raised $5,500 in total. The Family Business Association of California PAC gave $5,000 of the total.
The Yes campaign has raised $8,509 for every $1 of opposition dollars.
CTA, which led the signature drive to put Prop. 3 on the ballot, contributed $33.3 million – 71% of the total – while the CTA’s parent union, the National Education Association, donated $10 million. The California Federation of Teachers, the smaller of two California teachers unions, gave $1.75 million to go with the Service Employees International Union’s (SEIU) $1.5 million.
CTA’s elected 700-delegate State Council allocated the money in June, “not taking anything for granted,” said CTA President David Goldberg. CTA was less worried about the opposition than with the sheer number of 14 initiatives on the ballot. It’s been more important to raise awareness of Prop. 3 “above the noise,” he said.
Now, with five weeks to go before the election, he said, “I would assume there is enough for every scenario to win this,” including TV ads. ”It’s definitely an option.”
Two choices: a wealth tax and/or an income tax?
Prop. 3 is one of two tax-raising initiatives on the November ballot. The other, far more contentious one, is Prop. 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)), which would create the nation’s first tax on the net worth of the state’s 200-plus billionaires.
The independent, nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the one-time, 5% tax on most of the billionaires’ assets would yield tens of billions of dollars. But it also cautioned it could result in a loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue if the richest of the rich follow the lead of Elon Musk and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin and move out of state to cheaper tax states like Florida and Texas.
CTA opposes Prop. 40 because TK-12 and community colleges would receive only 10% of the take from Prop. 40, a smaller ratio than the 40% that they already get annually as their share of the state’s general fund revenue under a constitutional amendment passed in 1988.
Prop. 3 would continue that ratio. The LAO projects that, depending on volatile income and capital tax revenue, Prop. 3 would continue to bring in $5 billion to $15 billion to the general fund with 40% – $2 billion to $6 billion – going to schools and community colleges annually.
A Prop. 3 surcharge of 1% starts with taxable income of $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers. It would jump to an additional 3 percentage points for those single filers making more than $743,000 or $1.5 million for joint filers.
More than 50% support in a new voter survey
Conventional thinking of pollsters and veteran political observers is that multiple tax measures on the same ballot, especially complex initiatives like the wealth tax, could hurt the chances of all tax initiatives: Frustrated voters would throw up their hands and vote “no” across their ballots.
But, based on the Sept. 25 voter survey by the UC Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies, that doesn’t seem to be happening; voters appear to be heading in opposite directions in support for Prop. 3 and Prop. 40.
Compared with a prior survey in August, support for Prop. 3 rose to 54% in favor, 34% opposed, and 13% undecided.
Support for Prop. 40 had fallen from above 50% in August to 45% in favor, 42% against, and 13% undecided, amid an onslaught of anti-Prop. 40 TV ads.
Although Fremont offers a small sample size — Democrats outnumber Republicans three to one in the Alameda County city — canvassing teachers said they heard widespread support for Prop. 3.
Nicole Black, a veteran kindergarten teacher, said someone came to the door in about half of the 50 houses she visited, with 20 of those indicating support, some asking for more information, and no one outright saying no. William Jung, a high school teacher, reported fewer conversations but proportionally higher support.
Vicky Chon encountered only one no – a shirtless man working in his garage who dismissed her with a flip of the hand, saying, “No more taxes.” But a woman who had said through her Ring doorbell video camera that she was driving her father to an appointment later was working in her garden and said she was all in. And an elderly lady with patchy English said, yes, she would vote for it, too.
No one wanted more details of Prop. 3 or asked about the wealth tax, so Chon and colleagues didn’t have to bring it up. They could stay on message: Prop. 3 will continue an existing tax. Voting yes will keep the status quo and prevent future layoffs of teachers.
In the coming weeks, voters can expect to be inundated with tens of millions of dollars worth of ads for, but mainly against, Prop. 40. Opponents have already spent $87 million – 85% of the $219 million total (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) – compared with $32 million by the proponents.
Meanwhile, teachers will be going door to door every weekend, Goldberg said. “We always knew a lot would rest on our shoulders,” he said. “No other organization can match our capacity in every community.”

Top Takeaways
A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. Barrera, an ally of organized labor, is the president of the San Diego Unified school board and is running for state superintendent of public instruction.
To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.

I have a rich picture. Let me consider a few remaining questions that could tip the balance:

1. Is there any non-ideological, evidence-based reason to vote no that outweighs? Main candidates:
   a. Revenue volatility and budget rigidity — LAO's longstanding concern. But note: LAO didn't take a position; it noted ~40% to schools and reserves get some.
   b. Migration/behavioral response — Rauh/Shyu (mixed with Varner/Young). Even under Rauh's estimate, the tax raised substantial net revenue. And Prop 3 doesn't change current rates, so no new migration trigger; if anything, avoiding the uncertainty of an expiration may be neutral.
   c. Loss of leverage for school reform / declining enrollment — a real point, but the funding is per-student formula-based (LCFF), so declining enrollment reduces total needs; and the revenue also backfills Medi-Cal.
   d. The "temporariness" principle — a governance argument, but weak when the alternative is a ~$10B/yr hole during structural deficits and federal Medicaid cuts.

2. Also worth checking: does the state's structural deficit argue for keeping revenue? Yes: LAO projects deficits of $20-35B annually. Removing $5-15B in revenue in 2031 would worsen this substantially (partially offset by lower Prop 98 requirement).

3. Consider whether a "no" vote would lead to a replacement with a more stable/broad-based tax reform — historically unlikely in CA (needs 2/3 legislative vote for tax increases; voters have repeatedly rejected broad tax reforms like split roll (Prop 15, 2020)).

4. Distributional: the tax cut would go to the top 2% (average saving maybe $10-30k/yr for affected households); the cuts would fall on schools/healthcare used broadly, particularly by lower-income families. Regressive outcome of a "no" vote.

5. Fairness of framing: opponents say "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history" — technically it's not an increase relative to current law, but it is an increase relative to the scheduled 2031 law. Both true.

I'm fairly convinced that "yes" is the better answer on the merits: it maintains existing rates that are the backbone of the state budget, funds education and children's healthcare, affects only the top 2%, has no evidence of major tax flight over 14 years, and is supported by most nonpartisan policy analysts (SPUR yes; LAO neutral but describing the revenue as significant), major editorial boards (SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee), professional associations (CMA, PTA), and polls (54-58% yes).

The counterpoints (rigidity, volatility, permanence removing accountability leverage, spending problem) are real but weaker: the revenue is needed given structural deficits and federal cuts; volatility is partly addressed by reserve requirements (and Prop 2 on the same ballot); and if it fails the practical outcome is a big hole rather than reform.

Let me do one last check on a couple of items: (1) the SF Chronicle editorial's reasoning and any caveats; (2) whether the LAO or others flag that making the tax permanent would increase volatility risk in a possible stock-market downturn — and whether the state's reserve levels are adequate. Also (3) whether there's a serious argument that letting it expire in 2031 would coincide with declining school enrollment and thus reduced need.

Actually, I think I have enough. But given the instruction "do extensive research," let me do two more checks: the SF Chronicle editorial and a search on whether California's enrollment decline reduces the revenue need / whether school funding is at record levels (opponents' claim) plus PPIC's assessment of school funding adequacy.

Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.

Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.

With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.

So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.

In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.

So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.

In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

- **Most district-level declines in student enrollment are large and long lasting.** The typical multi-year decline persists over a decade or more and is greater than 20 percent.

I have a rich picture. Let me consider a few remaining questions that could tip the balance:

1. Is there any non-ideological, evidence-based reason to vote no that outweighs? Main candidates:
   a. Revenue volatility and budget rigidity — LAO's longstanding concern. But note: LAO didn't take a position; it noted ~40% to schools and reserves get some.
   b. Migration/behavioral response — Rauh/Shyu (mixed with Varner/Young). Even under Rauh's estimate, the tax raised substantial net revenue. And Prop 3 doesn't change current rates, so no new migration trigger; if anything, avoiding the uncertainty of an expiration may be neutral.
   c. Loss of leverage for school reform / declining enrollment — a real point, but the funding is per-student formula-based (LCFF), so declining enrollment reduces total needs; and the revenue also backfills Medi-Cal.
   d. The "temporariness" principle — a governance argument, but weak when the alternative is a ~$10B/yr hole during structural deficits and federal Medicaid cuts.

2. Also worth checking: does the state's structural deficit argue for keeping revenue? Yes: LAO projects deficits of $20-35B annually. Removing $5-15B in revenue in 2031 would worsen this substantially (partially offset by lower Prop 98 requirement).

3. Consider whether a "no" vote would lead to a replacement with a more stable/broad-based tax reform — historically unlikely in CA (needs 2/3 legislative vote for tax increases; voters have repeatedly rejected broad tax reforms like split roll (Prop 15, 2020)).

4. Distributional: the tax cut would go to the top 2% (average saving maybe $10-30k/yr for affected households); the cuts would fall on schools/healthcare used broadly, particularly by lower-income families. Regressive outcome of a "no" vote.

5. Fairness of framing: opponents say "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history" — technically it's not an increase relative to current law, but it is an increase relative to the scheduled 2031 law. Both true.

I'm fairly convinced that "yes" is the better answer on the merits: it maintains existing rates that are the backbone of the state budget, funds education and children's healthcare, affects only the top 2%, has no evidence of major tax flight over 14 years, and is supported by most nonpartisan policy analysts (SPUR yes; LAO neutral but describing the revenue as significant), major editorial boards (SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee), professional associations (CMA, PTA), and polls (54-58% yes).

The counterpoints (rigidity, volatility, permanence removing accountability leverage, spending problem) are real but weaker: the revenue is needed given structural deficits and federal cuts; volatility is partly addressed by reserve requirements (and Prop 2 on the same ballot); and if it fails the practical outcome is a big hole rather than reform.

Let me do one last check on a couple of items: (1) the SF Chronicle editorial's reasoning and any caveats; (2) whether the LAO or others flag that making the tax permanent would increase volatility risk in a possible stock-market downturn — and whether the state's reserve levels are adequate. Also (3) whether there's a serious argument that letting it expire in 2031 would coincide with declining school enrollment and thus reduced need.

Actually, I think I have enough. But given the instruction "do extensive research," let me do two more checks: the SF Chronicle editorial and a search on whether California's enrollment decline reduces the revenue need / whether school funding is at record levels (opponents' claim) plus PPIC's assessment of school funding adequacy.

Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

The SF Chronicle's editorial is quite thoughtful: it acknowledges the volatility and structural problems, notes it opposed Prop 55 in 2016 hoping to force tax reform (which didn't happen), but concludes California can't afford to further reduce ongoing funds for schools and healthcare — vote yes.

Now let me think about the balance and the counterfactual. Key considerations for the "no" side that deserve weight:
- PPIC notes enrollment declines could free $7.5B for schools even without new revenue; per-pupil spending is at record highs; outcomes remain weak. So the "schools face devastating cuts" claim is partially overstated — though a $5-15B revenue loss would still reduce the Prop 98 guarantee substantially (Prop 98 is formula-driven by revenue; losing PIT revenue lowers the guarantee).
- Also, per LAO, the state faces structural deficits of $20-35B, which means the revenue is arguably needed regardless.
- Note: revenue volatility: making the tax permanent while LAO warns of a possible stock market bubble. But a "no" vote doesn't reduce volatility now (rates apply through 2030 anyway); it would reduce revenue concentration in 2031.

Another key question: what happens if it fails? Proponents can re-qualify in 2028 or 2030 (CalMatters notes "the union will have two more chances"). So a "no" vote isn't necessarily a permanent loss of revenue; it could delay. But delay creates uncertainty and the political cost of another campaign; also the state would face a scheduled cliff, prompting preemptive cuts and possibly worse decisions.

Also, if the tax expires in 2031 without replacement, that's a ~$10B/yr tax cut concentrated on the top 2% during a period of structural deficits and federal Medicaid cuts — an outcome that most public-interest analysis (and the evidence on tax flight, which is small) suggests is worse for the median Californian than keeping the revenue.

Considering the empirical migration literature: Rauh/Shyu find erosion of ~45-56% of the "windfall" revenue in the first years from behavioral responses including migration; Varner/Young/Prohofsky find little migration. Even the pessimistic estimate implies the tax raised far more than half its static yield — and, critically, Prop 3 doesn't change rates relative to today, so no new behavioral response is triggered. The relevant question is whether keeping rates at 12.3% vs dropping to 9.3% in 2031 causes more high earners to leave than staying. Evidence suggests modest effects at the margin, and PPIC data show high-earner out-migration is relatively low in CA and those leaving are less affluent than those arriving.

On the merits of fiscal policy: California's tax structure is overly reliant on volatile capital gains income, and making that permanent entrenches the problem. But the alternative — a $10B hole — is worse absent a credible reform package, and none exists on this ballot. The Chronicle's reasoning captures it: Prop 3 doesn't fix the underlying flaws, but the state can't afford to cut ongoing funding for schools and healthcare now.

There's also the health-care dimension: federal H.R. 1 cuts to Medicaid threaten ~$30B/yr for California; Prop 3 sustains up to $2B/yr for children's/family Medi-Cal and frees General Fund money.

Distributionally, a "yes" preserves progressive taxation funding services used broadly; a "no" delivers a large tax cut to the top 2% and shifts the burden to service cuts or other taxes.

Weighing everything, I conclude "yes" is the better vote.

One more sanity check: is there any hidden "poison pill" in Prop 3 that makes it worse than a simple extension? Let's verify: Section 5 conflicting measures clause — could nullify another measure that "affects the tax rates for personal income" getting fewer yes votes. On this ballot, are there measures affecting personal income tax rates? Prop 40 (wealth tax — arguably not "tax rates for personal income"), Props 41/42 (prohibit certain new taxes; 41 concerns special taxes and Gann limit; 42 concerns property/wealth taxes). Some tax law professors argue Prop 42 could be read to nullify Prop 3; conversely Prop 3's clause might void Prop 42 if Prop 3 gets more yes votes. Prop 3 polls 54-58%; Prop 42 polls ~50-51%. If both pass and Prop 3 has more yes votes and a court finds them conflicting, Prop 42 (and its nullification of Prop 40) could be voided "in their entirety" — potentially allowing Prop 40 to take effect if it passed. But Prop 40 is polling below majority (42-46%), so likely fails anyway. This is a speculative second-order effect; the LAO didn't flag an interaction. It's a minor consideration and not decisive, but worth noting as a risk. Given Prop 40 is likely to fail anyway (and would be nullified by 41/42 regardless), the risk is limited.

Also, Prop 3's Section 7 proponent standing is standard.

I'm confident: answer "yes".

Considering the empirical migration literature: Rauh/Shyu find erosion of ~45-56% of the "windfall" revenue in the first years from behavioral responses including migration; Varner/Young/Prohofsky find little migration. Even the pessimistic estimate implies the tax raised far more than half its static yield — and, critically, Prop 3 doesn't change rates relative to today, so no new behavioral response is triggered. The relevant question is whether keeping rates at 12.3% vs dropping to 9.3% in 2031 causes more high earners to leave than staying. Evidence suggests modest effects at the margin, and PPIC data show high-earner out-migration is relatively low in CA and those leaving are less affluent than those arriving.
