But the alternative — a $10B hole — is worse absent a credible reform package, and none exists on this ballot. The Chronicle's reasoning captures it: Prop 3 doesn't fix the underlying flaws, but the state can't afford to cut ongoing funding for schools and healthcare now.

There's also the health-care dimension: federal H.R. 1 cuts to Medicaid threaten ~$30B/yr for California; Prop 3 sustains up to $2B/yr for children's/family Medi-Cal and frees General Fund money.

Distributionally, a "yes" preserves progressive taxation funding services used broadly; a "no" delivers a large tax cut to the top 2% and shifts the burden to service cuts or other taxes.

Weighing everything, I conclude "yes" is the better vote.

One more sanity check: is there any hidden "poison pill" in Prop 3 that makes it worse than a simple extension? Let's verify: Section 5 conflicting measures clause — could nullify another measure that "affects the tax rates for personal income" getting fewer yes votes. On this ballot, are there measures affecting personal income tax rates? Prop 40 (wealth tax — arguably not "tax rates for personal income"), Props 41/42 (prohibit certain new taxes; 41 concerns special taxes and Gann limit; 42 concerns property/wealth taxes). Some tax law professors argue Prop 42 could be read to nullify Prop 3; conversely Prop 3's clause might void Prop 42 if Prop 3 gets more yes votes. Prop 3 polls 54-58%; Prop 42 polls ~50-51%. If both pass and Prop 3 has more yes votes and a court finds them conflicting, Prop 42 (and its nullification of Prop 40) could be voided "in their entirety" — potentially allowing Prop 40 to take effect if it passed. But Prop 40 is polling below majority (42-46%), so likely fails anyway. This is a speculative second-order effect; the LAO didn't flag an interaction. It's a minor consideration and not decisive, but worth noting as a risk. Given Prop 40 is likely to fail anyway (and would be nullified by 41/42 regardless), the risk is limited.

Also, Prop 3's Section 7 proponent standing is standard.

I'm confident: answer "yes".

PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 3
PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS, HEALTHCARE AND OUR COMMUNITIES WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES.
Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone. Prop. 3 prevents millionaires and billionaires from getting a tax cut, and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms.
PROP. 3 PREVENTS BILLIONS IN CUTS TO OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE.
Without Prop. 3, California’s 8 million public school and community college students face billions in cuts, including teacher layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and bigger class sizes. Families could lose access to preventive healthcare and affordable prescription drugs, and the Medi-Cal coverage that millions of Californians rely on could be put at risk.
PROP. 3 ONLY EXTENDS THE CURRENT TAX RATES ON THE WEALTHIEST TOP 2%.
Prop. 3 maintains the income tax rates that the wealthiest Californians have paid for the past 15 years. If those tax rates are allowed to expire, it would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities. Proposition 3 keeps the existing rates on the top 2% of incomes.
GUARANTEES THE MONEY REACHES THE CLASSROOM— NOT SACRAMENTO.
Proposition 3 includes Constitutional protections and tough accountability. It guarantees that funds from Proposition 3 go directly to local schools—the Legislature and Sacramento politicians cannot touch it, redirect it, or spend a single dollar on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Prop. 3’s school guarantee then frees up billions that help fund Medi-Cal for children, seniors and families.
Every dollar in Prop. 3 is independently audited every year and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties. Local school districts must post annual accounting online to guarantee that Californians know exactly how and where funds are spent.
PROP. 3 SECURES OUR CHILDREN’S FUTURE.
For more than a decade, these revenues have helped fund critical programs California families and communities count on—from school lunches, smaller class sizes and mental health counselors to children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal. They’ve also helped stave off cuts during economic downturns by investing more in the state’s Rainy Day Fund, protecting our schools and healthcare when the economy slows. Proposition 3 keeps that progress going for the next generation.
PROP. 3 IS SUPPORTED BY TEACHERS, NURSES, AND HEALTHCARE WORKERS.
Yes on 3 is supported by:
California State PTA
California Federation of Teachers
California Nurses Association
California School Employees Association
California School Nurses Organization
California Teachers Association
Community College League of California
Nurse Alliance of SEIU California
Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA
The educators in our classrooms and the nurses who care for our kids all agree: Vote YES on Proposition 3. Let’s protect what matters most, without raising your taxes. Vote YES on Proposition 3.
www.YesProp3CA.com
David Goldberg , President
California Teachers Association
Katie Nilsson , RN, President
California School Nurses Organization
Jodi Hicks , President
Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 3
NO ON PROP. 3—STOP PERMANENTLY HIGHER INCOME TAXES
In 2012, politicians and special interests promised Californians that their income tax increases would be TEMPORARY. Now they’re claiming that making those taxes permanent somehow ISN’T a tax increase at all. Don’t buy it. Prop. 3 locks in what would become the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history— costing taxpayers up to $15 billion every year.
NO ON PROP. 3—REMIND POLITICIANS WHAT “TEMPORARY” MEANS
Temporary: lasting for a limited time only; not permanent.
California taxpayers kept their end of the bargain—paying temporary higher income taxes for 16 years. Politicians should keep theirs and stop pushing for even higher taxes.
NO ON PROP. 3—STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING
Prop. 3 does nothing to stop the waste, fraud and reckless spending that turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion deficit in just three years. If Sacramento had spent responsibly, they wouldn’t be asking taxpayers to make “temporary” taxes permanent.
NO ON PROP. 3—DON’T MAKE CALIFORNIA EVEN MORE EXPENSIVE
Californians have the highest cost of living and pay the highest income, sales and gas taxes in America. Making a temporary tax permanent only makes California more expensive.
NO ON PROP. 3—FIX THE SPENDING PROBLEM FIRST
California doesn’t have a tax revenue problem—it has a spending problem. California’s population grew by less than 2% in the past decade while the politicians doubled spending. Say no to permanently higher taxes. Join us to oppose higher income taxes at VoteNoProp3.com .
NO ON PROP. 3
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Carlos Solorzano , CEO
Hispanic Chambers of Commerce of San Francisco
Clint Olivier , President
Central Valley Business Federation
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 3
PROP. 3-TURNS "TEMPORARY" TAXES INTO PERMANENT HIGHER INCOME TAXES
Sacramento politicians make big promises to get our support for higher taxes. Then they spend our tax dollars with no accountability-losing billions to waste, fraud and overspending.
Take Prop. 3. Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary-only for seven years to cover a budget deficit. Then those "temporary" taxes were extended for another 12 years with the promise to voters that the higher taxes would solve the problems the politicians created. Now the special interests and politicians want to make these higher income taxes PERMANENT.
California voters should say NO to PERMANENTLY higher income taxes.
PROP. 3-HIGHER INCOME TAXES = HIGHER COST OF LIVING
Californians have the nation's highest cost of living partly because we also suffer from the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes of all fifty states. The same politicians also gave us the highest gasoline prices in the nation, higher insurance costs, higher utility costs, higher food costs, and higher housing costs. Now they want to make higher income taxes permanent, while adding new taxes on your health insurance, new taxes on software-and they are even considering a "jobs" tax. Say NO to INCREASING our cost of living with higher taxes.
PROP. 3-VOTERS DESERVE REAL RESULTS, NOT BROKEN PROMISES
Waste, fraud and overspending by state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.
The politicians and special interests promised temporary income taxes were needed to avoid big cuts to government programs. Since the "temporary" increases were first passed, government spending has increased by $150 billion-a more than 2.5X increase. Over the same time period, our schools, infrastructure and public safety have gotten worse. Say NO to endless broken promises.
NO ON PROP. 3-STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING
The politicians and special interests turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years. They mismanaged our tax dollars so badly, they now want voters to bail them out with permanently higher taxes.
Say NO to $100 billion wasted on a train to nowhere.
Say NO to $37 billion wasted on homeless programs that don't work.
Say NO to $31 billion wasted on unemployment fraud.
NO ON PROP. 3-FIX SACRAMENTO'S SPENDING PROBLEM BEFORE RAISING TAXES
California doesn't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem. California's population barely grew in the past 10 years, but the politicians more than doubled spending.
It's not just state taxes that keep going up. Politicians and special interests have imposed more than 2,000 new local tax increases in just the past ten years-making it much harder for struggling Californians to make ends meet.
Californians shouldn't support any higher taxes until we get spending under control.
STOP WASTEFUL SPENDING.
NO NEW TAXES.
NO ON PROP. 3.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Robert Rivinius , President
Family Business Association of California

Proposition 3 protects our schools, our healthcare and our communities—without raising your taxes.
PROP. 3 KEEPS THE TAX RATES THE TOP 2% HAVE PAID FOR THE PAST 15 YEARS AND DOES NOT RAISE YOUR TAXES.
Prop. 3 maintains the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% of Californians have been paying for 15 years, ensuring couples that earn more than $740,000 continue to pay their fair share.
WITHOUT PROP. 3 MILLIONAIRES AND BILLIONAIRES GET A MASSIVE TAX CUT—AND THE REST OF US PAY FOR IT.
Teacher and staff layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and fewer counselors in our schools; cuts to Medi-Cal, children’s healthcare and the clinics families rely on; and less for the firefighters, emergency response and wildfire protection that keep our communities safe.
PROP. 3 HAS STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND FUNDS EDUCATION DIRECTLY.
Prop. 3’s funding goes straight to local schools and community colleges. Sacramento politicians cannot touch it or redirect it. Not one penny may be spent on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Every dollar is independently audited every year, districts must post their spending online, and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties.
PROP. 3 PROTECTS HEALTHCARE AND FIRE PROTECTION.
By guaranteeing funding for our classrooms, Prop. 3 ensures California can also invest in Medi-Cal and children’s healthcare, and in the firefighters and wildfire protection our communities depend on. That’s why teachers, school employees, nurses and firefighters agree: VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 3.

PROPOSED LAW
The California Children’s Education and Health Care
Protection Act of 2026
SECTION 1. Title.
This measure shall be known and may be cited as “The
California Children’s Education and Health Care
Protection Act of 2026.”
SEC. 2. Findings.
Text of Proposed Laws | 109
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 3 CONTINUED
(a) In 2012, California voters passed a tax increase on
high-income earners—the top 2%—to fund critical
state services and stave off extreme cuts to public
education brought on by the fiscal challenges of the
Great Recession. These tax rates were extended by the
voters in 2016, with 63% voting yes. Since its initial
passage, this tax measure has raised more than $104
billion for schools and other essential services. It is a
foundational part of the state budget and the state
Rainy Day Fund.
3 (b) This high-earner income tax has allowed the state
to make important investments in the education and
health of our children and has helped California’s
public school system become more competitive among
the 50 states. In 2012, California ranked in the bottom
10 among the states in school spending. Today, with
these revenues, California has made real progress in
school spending. Our state now provides free school
meals; free transitional kindergarten to all four-year-
olds; free before-and-after school care for younger
elementary students; and community services in many
school districts.
(c) Unless the tax is extended by the voters, it will
expire in 2030. That would result in an immediate
reduction to state revenues of over $10 billion and
devastating cuts to schools, children’s health care, and
other essential services. It would reverse the gains our
schools have made since the initial passage of the high-
earner income tax in 2012.
(d) This measure does not increase taxes on couples
earning less than $680,000 or individuals earning less
than $340,000, in today’s dollars. It does not change
the existing tax rates, which have remained the same
since this tax measure was first enacted in 2012.
(e) This is not the time to be giving the wealthiest
people in California a tax cut that they don’t need and
that our schools and communities can’t afford.
Maintaining this tax on high earners helps ensure that
California children receive the education and health
care they need to thrive and achieve their highest
potential, while allowing this tax to expire would require
major cuts to the education and health of our next
generation.
(f) California’s future depends on the success of its
over 9 million children. Every California child deserves
a fair chance to become a successful adult. But for
children to succeed as adults, they must have access
to high quality education and health care.
(g) For children, education and health care are
essential and dependent on one another. Access to a
quality education is fundamental to the success of
California’s children. Even with adequate schools,
children cannot obtain an education if illness prevents
them from attending. And children growing up in
communities without adequate health care are more
likely to contract illnesses or have chronic medical
conditions that prevent them from regularly attending
school.
(h) Research shows that early access to quality
education and health care improves children’s chances
110 | Text of Proposed Laws
of succeeding in school and in life. This tax on high
earners helps ensure that California children receive
the education and health care they need to thrive and
achieve their highest potential.
(i) The income tax revenue is guaranteed in the
California Constitution to go directly to local school
districts and community colleges. State funding is freed
up to help balance the budget and provide for a Rainy
Day Fund to prevent cuts to health care for children
and their families; services for seniors, working
families, and small business owners; wildfire
prevention; and other critical needs even when
revenues decline. Everyone benefits.
(j) To ensure all these funds go only where the voters
intend, they are put in a special fund that the
Legislature cannot divert to other purposes. None of
these revenues can be spent on state bureaucracy or
administrative costs.
(k) These funds are subject to an independent audit
every year to ensure they are spent only for the
purposes set forth in this measure. Elected officials will
be subject to prosecution and criminal penalties if they
misuse the funds.
(l) This measure helped build and will sustain the
state’s Rainy Day Fund. California has seen massive
budget swings over the past 15 years, with good years
often followed by deep deficits and devastating cuts.
Maintaining the state’s Rainy Day Fund has helped
protect our children, seniors, and disabled Californians
from cuts in school and health care funding during
economic downturns.
(m) Federal budget cuts will have a huge impact on
low-income Californians, and especially on our
children. But federal tax laws are giving huge tax breaks
to wealthy taxpayers. Maintaining this existing tax on
high-earning Californians is essential to protecting our
schools and our school children.
SEC. 3. Purpose and Intent.
(a) The chief purpose and intent of the voters in
enacting this measure is to avoid harmful cuts that
would reduce the quality of education and instruction
in California’s local public schools, and to provide
adequate funding for essential health care services for
children and their family members.
(b) This measure is intended to protect our children by
extending current income tax rates on wealthy
Californians. Instead of sending money back into the
pockets of the wealthy, this measure sends the money
to a special account that must be spent exclusively to
ensure that every California child has access to a
quality public education. This frees up state funding to
provide health care for children and fund other
essential services.
(c) This measure guarantees in the Constitution that
the revenues it raises for schools will be sent directly to
school districts and community colleges for classroom
expenses, not administrative costs. This school funding
cannot be suspended or withheld no matter what
happens with the state budget.

Prop
3
|
Constitutional Amendment
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
Makes permanent the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to fund education, healthcare, and other state programs.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 3 would make permanent an existing high-earner tax that funds K–12/community college education, children’s healthcare, and debt paydown. This tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, with no evidence that it has driven high earners out of state. It’s highly progressive, hitting only top earners while sustaining programs such as universal school meals that disproportionately benefit low-income students, and it would help backfill Medi-Cal funding just as federal cuts threaten healthcare access for millions of low-income Californians. The trade-offs are modest: permanence would limit future tax flexibility, and reliance on capital-gains-linked income would keep revenue volatile. But given the tax's proven track record and the increasingly dramatic funding gaps the tax would help fill in the wake of H.R. 1, SPUR supports making it permanent.
Vote YES
What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030. In 2025, the top 2% income bracket started at $371,001 a year for individuals and $743,001 a year for couples filing jointly. The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.
Revenue would primarily support K–12 schools and community colleges under 1988’s Proposition 98. About 40% — $2 billion to $6 billion annually — would go to education, while remaining funds could support children’s healthcare, the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund), and other General Fund uses. Because the revenue counts toward the state’s required education funding, it frees up General Fund dollars for other programs. 1
If the tax rates set in 2012 expire, the state would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually. 2 In the short term, the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements; over time, the Proposition 98-mandated spending minimum could decline depending on the formula in use, economic conditions, and legislative decisions.
The Backstory
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country (meaning the tax rate is higher the more income one earns). Voters approved Prop. 30 in 2012 to temporarily raise rates on high earners, then extended it through Prop. 55 in 2016 (expiring in 2030). Before Prop. 30, the top rate was 9.3%.
The tax structure for the top 2% of earners in California under different scenarios depends on whether Prop. 3 passes.

Prop. 98 requires California to provide a minimum level of funding for K–12 schools and community colleges each year, based on state revenues, economic growth, and student enrollment. Local property taxes also contribute to the Prop. 98 minimum. Together, these requirements typically direct about 40% of General Fund revenues to education. 3
Of the education funding, 89% goes to K–12 schools and 11% to community colleges. None of the funding can be used for administrative costs. After meeting education requirements, revenues go to debt service and the rainy day fund; 50% of remaining funds, capped at $2 billion annually, may support Medi-Cal children’s and family health services.
Medi-Cal provides free or low-cost health care to nearly 15 million Californians. This funding is especially important after federal bill H.R. 1 made major cuts to health care and food assistance. Federal Medicaid cuts could cost Medi-Cal tens of billions of dollars annually and cause up to 2 million Californians to lose coverage.
Since January 1, 2012, the top-earner income tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, helping more than double school funding and support transitional kindergarten, expanded learning, free school meals, COVID-19 recovery, and teacher recruitment. 4 Before the passage of Prop. 30, California ranked 50th among states in per-student education spending. Now it ranks 16th (or 31st when accounting for the state’s cost of living). 5 However, because 80% of school spending goes to staff salaries and benefits, the state still has 22 students per teacher, compared with 15.4 nationally. 6
Recently, the tax has generated about $9 billion to $10 billion annually, although revenues fluctuate with the economy and stock market. The LAO estimates annual revenues could range from $5 billion to $15 billion.
Notably, high earners have not fled the state because of this tax; California has had the second-lowest out-migration rate among $200,000-plus households of any state over the past decade. 7 The state has lost less-educated and lower-income adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults because of affordability and cost-of-living concerns. 8
Californians for Protecting Public Education, Health Care and Budget Stability led the effort to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, with funding from the California Teachers Association and California Federation of Teachers. Some proponents oppose Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax, out of concern that it could undermine support for Prop. 3.
A citizen-initiated measure, Prop. 3 needs a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Allowing the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to expire would require major cuts to education spending on the next generation of Californians, which would disproportionately impact low-income children and students of color. This income tax revenue enabled California to become the first state offering free breakfast and lunch to all TK–12 students, plus free after-school programs prioritizing low-income neighborhoods.
California’s educational funding formula, the Local Control Funding Formula, directs the most resources to students who face the greatest educational hurdles, including grants for English learners, foster youth, homeless students, and low-income families in high-poverty districts. 9
Prop. 3 would backfill federal cuts and sustain up to $2 billion in annual funding for Medi-Cal, most of which goes to low-income people and people of color. Without state budget and policy intervention, the cuts from H.R. 1 are expected to completely destabilize California’s healthcare and hospital system, exacerbate food insecurity, and cause children to miss routine screenings and vaccines. 10
The measure is highly progressive; it does not increase taxes on couples earning less than $743,001 or individuals earning less than $341,001, in today’s dollars.
Pros
Prop. 3 would help backfill ongoing funding needs for children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal, which is facing severe federal funding cuts.
The measure would tax only California’s highest earners.
It would not increase the current income tax rate, which was set in 2012.
Any leftover capital-gains-driven revenue would lower state debt and help build the rainy day fund, which supports the state’s financial health and mitigates the volatility of this funding source.
There is no evidence that the tax has contributed to any significant tax flight from the state.
Because the tax is permanent, it would facilitate greater predictability in state revenues.
Cons
The state’s reliance on taxing the highest income earners would increase state budget volatility.
The measure is restrictive: it would require meeting the Prop. 98 education minimum before allowing flexibility in funding allocation.
Vote YES

A.G. File No. 2025-016
October 20, 2025
PDF Version (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250421.pdf)
Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed constitutional initiative that maintains personal income tax rates for high-income taxpayers (A.G. File No. 25-0016).
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Personal Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for the majority of spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Recent Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend This Money? The state collects taxes from people and businesses and uses them to pay for services to the public. This year, the state plans to spend about $230 billion from the General Fund. About half of this spending is for K-12 schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The amount spent on K-12 schools and community colleges is set by the State Constitution.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's health insurance program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, parole programs, and courts.
Proposal
This measure maintains the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 by making them permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Measure Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by this measure is hard to predict and will go up and down with the economy. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing investment income and capital gains. These types of income are closely tied to the stock market and therefore go up and down a lot from year to year. In a weak year, the measure might bring in around $5 billion in revenue. In a strong year, the measure might bring in $15 billion in annual revenue. In most years, revenue brought in by the measure would be in between these amounts. These amounts are in today's dollars and would tend to grow over time.
A Large Portion of the Money Would Go to Schools and Community Colleges. The State Constitution requires the state to spend a large portion of new money on schools and community colleges. Typically, about 40 percent of the revenue brought in by this measure would go to schools and community colleges.
A Smaller Portion of the Money Would Go to Reserves. The State Constitution requires the state to set aside money to save in budget reserves. Reserves help the state balance its budget when the economy is weak and revenues decline. Some of the money brought in under this measure would be saved in reserves. This means the state would have more money in savings to balance the budget when the economy is weak.
Remaining Money Could Be Spent on Other State Programs. Money brought in under this measure that does not go to schools, community colleges, or reserves could be used for other state programs.
Summary of Fiscal Effects. We estimate the measure would have the following major fiscal effects:
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income taxes (in today's dollars) by making a tax on high income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

content.thinking:
Let me look at the opposing side arguments more carefully: San Diego Union-Tribune editorial (no), OC Register editorial (no), CalMatters commentary against, and also research on revenue volatility and migration effects. Also, key issue: the "conflicting measures" clause in Prop 3 — does it affect Prop 40/41/42? Let's check news coverage on that.

Also, one nuance: Prop 3's text apparently doesn't actually "guarantee" funds directly to schools in a new way; it makes permanent Prop 30's Education Protection Account provisions. Wait — under Prop 55, the revenue did NOT go into the Education Protection Account; Prop 55 revenues went to the General Fund with Prop 98 formula. Prop 30 had the Education Protection Account with 89%/11% split and the healthcare carve-out (50% of excess above Prop 98 minimum + workload budget, up to $2B, to DHCS). Prop 3 appears to restore/permanently extend Article XIII Section 36 as originally written in Prop 30 (amending the sunset dates). So the Education Protection Account mechanism would be permanent: 89% K-12, 11% CCC, up to $2B to children's Medi-Cal.

Hmm, but note that the LAO says roughly 40% goes to schools and community colleges. That's because revenue counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee, so the Education Protection Account funds are largely counted as part of Prop 98 minimum — meaning the extra money to schools beyond what Prop 98 requires is smaller. Actually, the EPA allocation mechanism gives 89/11 of revenues to schools/community colleges as "general purpose funding" which counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee; the state must still meet the guarantee from other funds. Net effect: schools get about 40% of revenue per LAO (the Prop 98 minimum share). This is an important nuance where the proponents' claim "funds go directly to classrooms" is partly true mechanically but the net fiscal benefit to schools is ~40%.

Also there's the interaction with Prop 98: making revenue permanent raises the Prop 98 guarantee permanently, reducing flexibility. Also the volatility issue: high-income tax revenues are volatile; permanent reliance deepens volatility. Though Prop 2 (rainy day fund) is also on the ballot, which would strengthen reserves.

Consider migration/economic effects: PPIC and others find minimal migration effect for the top 2% from Prop 30/55 — CA has had second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households. But some argue permanence at a time when other states cut taxes and federal tax changes (OBBBA raising SALT cap to $40k) change the calculus. The 13.3% top rate (with mental health surtax) is highest in nation; combined with federal, high earners in CA face ~50%+ marginal rates. There's evidence of modest elasticity among top earners (Kleven/Landais: small but non-zero migration elasticity for top earners; more relevant: capital gains timing/realization shifts). Also 2024's Prop 2? Not relevant.

Let me also check the "conflicting measures" clause analysis — this is a significant consideration. If Prop 3 passes with more votes than Prop 40, does Prop 40 get nullified? Prop 40 is a one-time excise tax on net worth, not a "tax rate for personal income," so probably not a conflict. But Props 41 and 42 (billionaire countermeasures) — Prop 41 (tax audits) and Prop 42 (prohibits new state property taxes)? Let me look at what these are. The LA Times said "Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40 from becoming law even if voters pass it." Hmm. Prop 3's conflicting-measure clause could nullify Prop 41/42 if Prop 3 gets more votes — but that only matters if they conflict on "tax rates for personal income."

Also, one nuance: Prop 3's text apparently doesn't actually "guarantee" funds directly to schools in a new way; it makes permanent Prop 30's Education Protection Account provisions. Wait — under Prop 55, the revenue did NOT go into the Education Protection Account; Prop 55 revenues went to the General Fund with Prop 98 formula. Prop 30 had the Education Protection Account with 89%/11% split and the healthcare carve-out (50% of excess above Prop 98 minimum + workload budget, up to $2B, to DHCS). Prop 3 appears to restore/permanently extend Article XIII Section 36 as originally written in Prop 30 (amending the sunset dates). So the Education Protection Account mechanism would be permanent: 89% K-12, 11% CCC, up to $2B to children's Medi-Cal.

Hmm, but note that the LAO says roughly 40% goes to schools and community colleges. That's because revenue counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee, so the Education Protection Account funds are largely counted as part of Prop 98 minimum — meaning the extra money to schools beyond what Prop 98 requires is smaller. Actually, the EPA allocation mechanism gives 89/11 of revenues to schools/community colleges as "general purpose funding" which counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee; the state must still meet the guarantee from other funds. Net effect: schools get about 40% of revenue per LAO (the Prop 98 minimum share). This is an important nuance where the proponents' claim "funds go directly to classrooms" is partly true mechanically but the net fiscal benefit to schools is ~40%.

Also there's the interaction with Prop 98: making revenue permanent raises the Prop 98 guarantee permanently, reducing flexibility. Also the volatility issue: high-income tax revenues are volatile; permanent reliance deepens volatility. Though Prop 2 (rainy day fund) is also on the ballot, which would strengthen reserves.

Consider migration/economic effects: PPIC and others find minimal migration effect for the top 2% from Prop 30/55 — CA has had second-lowest out-migration rate among $200k+ households. Both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, the most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years, saw evaluating teacher effectiveness as a much-needed education reform. This shows Clinton walking with then-President Obama as they golfed in Maryland in 2011. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

Interesting nuance: Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause vs. Props 40/41/42. And tax law professors note Prop 42 might undermine Prop 3. But Prop 3 has its own conflict clause: if Prop 3 gets more yes votes than a conflicting measure affecting personal income tax rates, Prop 3 prevails. Prop 3 polls at 54-58% yes; Prop 41/42 poll around 50-51%. So Prop 3 likely gets more yes votes than 41/42 → Prop 3 would prevail over them if deemed conflicting. That's a legal question.

Now, for a decision, let me weigh:

Pro-yes considerations:
1. Revenue: $5-15B/year, essential to state budget; expiry would force ~$10B+ in cuts or new taxes.
2. Rates only affect top 2%; no tax increase relative to current law (though relative to what would otherwise happen after 2031, it is an increase).
3. Empirical evidence: minimal migration effect from Prop 30/55 over 14 years; CA out-migration among high earners is low; PPIC data.
4. Federal cuts (H.R. 1) to Medi-Cal create new funding needs; Prop 3 backfills up to $2B/year for children's healthcare.
5. Accountability provisions: Education Protection Account, no administrative costs, annual audits, online posting.
6. Broad support: teachers, nurses, PTA, CMA, Democratic Party; editorial boards SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee; SPUR yes; polls 54-58% yes.
7. Progressive tax structure: revenue volatility is partly mitigated by rainy day fund; and Prop 2 on same ballot strengthens reserves.

Pro-no considerations:
1. Permanence locks in the state's highest-in-nation top marginal rate (13.3% with MHST), reducing future flexibility; makes structural reliance on volatile capital gains revenue permanent.
2. "Temporary" promise broken; precedent of moving goalposts.
3. No urgency — the tax doesn't expire until end of 2030; the Legislature/voters could decide in 2028 or 2030 with better information; deciding now forgoes leverage for reform (e.g., school accountability, cost control).
4. California's affordability crisis and out-migration of lower/middle-income residents; high taxes on top earners arguably contribute to cost of living, business climate; risk that permanence accelerates departure of high earners, especially combined with Prop 40 uncertainty and federal SALT cap changes.
5. Declining K-12 enrollment: spending per pupil at record high while outcomes remain mediocre; permanent dedication of revenue reduces flexibility to reallocate.
6. The initiative's dedication to the EPA and the conflict clause may interact with other measures (Props 41/42) creating legal uncertainty.
7. Constitutional amendments that permanently dedicate revenue are generally considered bad budget practice (LAO has criticized "lockbox" measures and rigidity).

Now, which is "better"? Let me think about the strongest analytical considerations. Let me dig a bit more into the migration evidence and the fiscal impact of letting it expire. Also, whether the state would actually cut $10B or replace it. And the LAO's assessment of Prop 98 implications: if revenue falls, Prop 98 minimum falls too, so cuts to schools would be moderated. The LAO's analysis says roughly 40% to schools.

Consider also: is it better policy to make the rate permanent vs. letting it expire and possibly replacing with a broader tax? California's income tax reliance on top earners is extreme (top 1% pay ~40-50% of income tax). Volatility caused big swings (2023 $30B+ shortfall driven by capital gains). Permanence entrenches that. But the counterargument: the rates already exist through 2030, and the state budget now structurally depends on them; letting them lapse would force deep cuts or new taxes at a worse time. There's no serious proposal to replace them with a less volatile tax.

Also, note the fiscal context in 2026: California has deficits and federal cuts to Medi-Cal. If Prop 3 fails, the state loses $5-15B annually starting 2031, which would be roughly a 4-6% General Fund cut.

Let me look at a few more sources: the CalMatters "What to know about Prop 3" article, the LA Times guide, and the opposition commentary (CalMatters commentary against). Also check whether any credible centrist group (e.g., PPIC, Bay Area Council, Chamber of Commerce) opposed. And the "Yes on 3" funding sources (CTA). Also check any analysis of whether Prop 3 could cause wealth managers/high earners to relocate — e.g., evidence from New Jersey's millionaire tax, from California's Prop 30 studies.

Let me fetch the CalMatters commentary against and the CalMatters Prop 3 explainer.

If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. An income tax on California’s highest earners, first passed in 2012, will expire in five years unless voters make the levy for school funding permanent. Below, an anti-tax advocate argues California’s pattern of making temporary taxes permanent is bad policy, and voters can break the cycle. The opposing view: A cafeteria manager says students and families will be hit hardest (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) if Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) fails. Guest Commentary written by Robert Gutierrez Robert Gutierrez is president of the California Taxpayers Association. For more than a century, California’s tax system has followed a familiar pattern: A fiscal crisis emerges, government responds with a “temporary” tax increase, the crisis passes and the tax remains. Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would continue this troubling pattern by making a “temporary” tax increase permanent. Supporters of Prop. 3 argue that the measure will provide ongoing funding for two priorities of most Californians, education and healthcare. The question is not whether those services matter — clearly, they do — but whether it is a sound policy to permanently extend tax hikes that voters were repeatedly told would expire. When California voters approved higher personal income tax rates in 2012, they were told the increase was a short-term emergency response to a specific fiscal challenge. Four years later, voters were asked to extend the tax increases, again for a limited time. Prop. 3 would make the tax hikes permanent — during a year in which high taxes and the unaffordable cost of living are the biggest problems for the majority of Californians. A recent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) found that roughly half of Californians say the cost of living is their top concern, and 55% prefer lower taxes and fewer government services. The reason that “temporary” tax hikes rarely disappear is that once government adjusts its spending to the higher revenue, politicians and special interests treat this as the new baseline. It doesn’t have to be this way. By rejecting Prop. 3, California voters can break the tradition and make sure that a temporary tax truly is temporary. READ NEXT Commentary (https://calmatters.org/category/commentary/) Proposition 3 sustains California schools. Losing the high-income tax would be devastating (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/proposition-3-california-schools-funding/) It is worth noting that California’s new state budget establishes record-high education spending of $27,418 per pupil (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/TK-12Education.pdf), up 27% from just five years earlier (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2021-22/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/K-12Education.pdf). Public schools continue to be the state’s top priority, receiving roughly 46% of the state’s general fund budget (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/BudgetSummary/SummaryCharts.pdf). Additionally, the entire budget reached a record high of $351.7 billion in spending, an $89 billion increase in spending (34%) from five years ago. In other words, any fiscal emergency of the past has been addressed. Supporters characterize Prop. 3 as affecting only high-income taxpayers, but it is not that simple. California’s tax system does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S corporations, reporting business earnings on personal income tax returns. As a result, extending higher tax rates would sustain higher costs for many small businesses — ultimately resulting in higher prices for their customers. The broader economic effects deserve scrutiny, as well. California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and has the highest state sales tax rate and gas tax. The state applies an additional 1.3% tax on all wage income to pay for the State Disability Insurance program. In addition to keeping costs high in California, Prop. 3 would deepen California’s reliance on the state’s most volatile revenue source: taxes paid by high-income earners (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/#5dfdd7c1-ccba-4770-802a-ec01052bfd71). During economic expansions, revenue surges. During downturns, revenue can fall dramatically, leaving the state struggling to pay ongoing expenses — especially when the demand for public services is increasing. Expanding permanent spending commitments tied to the most volatile revenue stream reduces flexibility when the economy weakens. Education and healthcare deserve stable funding. But stable funding should rest on honest budgeting and prioritizing the ample resources already available — not on repeatedly extending taxes that voters were assured would expire. content.thinking:
Good — this is a genuinely contested empirical question. Rauh/Shyu find meaningful behavioral erosion (~45-56% of expected windfall revenue eroded in first years, and 0.8pp increase in departure rate for the top bracket), while Varner/Young/Prohofsky find little migration response. Note that even if revenue eroded 45-56%, the tax still raised substantial revenue ($104B+ cumulative per proponents; Controller's tracking site). So the behavioral response reduces but doesn't eliminate revenue. And notably, the "erosion" estimate means the state collects roughly half of the static estimate — which is still $5-10B/yr.

Also important: LAO's estimates of $5-15B presumably account for some behavioral response? Not necessarily.

Now, the state's fiscal situation: LAO projects structural deficits of $20-35 billion annually starting 2027-28. In that context, letting $5-15B of revenue lapse in 2031 would deepen the structural gap; alternatively, a "no" vote gives the Legislature pressure to reform spending. Note that the LAO says the problem is structural — spending growth outstrips revenue growth — and even with record PIT revenues there are deficits. Hmm, that's an argument that Prop 3 alone doesn't solve the structural problem, but it doesn't follow that losing $10B/year would help.

One important nuance: Because of Prop 98 and Prop 2 (2014), revenue increases get largely offset by constitutionally required spending on schools and reserves — LAO noted "constitutional spending requirements under Proposition 98 and Proposition 2 almost entirely offset revenue gains." So a "yes" vote keeps $5-15B, but roughly 40%+ goes to schools automatically, ~some to reserves, and the rest to other programs. If the tax expires, Prop 98 minimum would decline correspondingly, meaning schools would absorb ~40% of the loss through the formula, so the hit to the rest of the budget would be ~60% of the loss. Still large.

Let me consider the strongest arguments:

Yes case:
- The state faces a structural deficit; losing $5-15B/yr (about 4-6% of General Fund) starting in 2031 would force deep cuts to education, healthcare, and other services, or new broad-based taxes. Given federal Medicaid cuts (H.R. 1) hitting California (estimated $30B/yr loss to Medi-Cal per SFGate), the fiscal need is acute.
- The tax is highly progressive, hitting only top 2%, who pay about half of income tax. Empirical evidence on migration is mixed but the tax has been in place 14 years without an exodus; PPIC finds those leaving CA are less affluent than those moving in; CBPP finds state taxes have minimal impact on interstate moves.
- No new tax: rates stay as they've been since 2013. Voting no means a tax cut for the top 2% of ~$10B/yr that the state cannot afford.
- Accountability: EPA dedicated 89/11 to K-12/CCC, no admin costs, audits.
- Broad coalition support (CTA, PTA, CMA, nurses, firefighters, CA Democratic Party); most major editorial boards in favor; polls 54-58% yes.

No case:
- Permanence eliminates voter/legislative leverage; temporary taxes force periodic reevaluation. There's no urgency since expiration is 2031; a decision could be deferred to 2028/2030 (and if it fails now, proponents can re-qualify).
- Deepens reliance on the most volatile revenue source at a moment when LAO warns of a stock-market bubble and structural deficits; permanence reduces budget flexibility.
- California's top rate 13.3% is the highest in the nation; combined with federal and other taxes it's near the top globally; evidence (Rauh/Shyu) of behavioral erosion, which is a real cost, plus risk of accelerating out-migration of high earners and entrepreneurs, especially given Prop 40's chilling effect and other states (Texas, Florida, Nevada, Washington) recruiting businesses.
- Small business pass-through income is affected (S-corps, partnerships), raising costs for businesses and consumers.
- Spending per pupil is at a record high ($27,418) while outcomes remain mediocre; enrollment declining ~500k students; no reforms attached to the money. Locking in funding without accountability for results (SDUT argument).
- The initiative's rigid dedication reduces the Legislature's flexibility, and the conflict clause adds legal uncertainty interacting with Props 40/41/42.

How to weigh? Consider a median-voter/public-interest framework. Key considerations:

1. Is the revenue needed? Almost certainly yes given structural deficits and federal cuts. But "no" doesn't automatically mean revenue disappears — it could be re-authorized in 2028 or 2030. However, waiting creates uncertainty for school budgeting and would likely trigger preemptive cuts before 2031. Also, history shows extension measures passed comfortably in 2016 (63%). So the practical difference between yes now and yes in 2030 is mostly about timing certainty and the political capital spent.

2. Is permanence bad? Per se, permanence of a well-functioning, highly progressive tax that has not caused a measurable exodus is not obviously harmful. However, budget scholars (LAO) have long criticized ballot-box budgeting and rigid dedications. But Prop 3's dedication is essentially the same mechanism as Prop 30's, already in place.

3. Volatility: A real concern, but Prop 3 does route excess to reserves; and the alternative (expiry) doesn't reduce volatility of the remaining tax base — California's PIT concentration exists regardless. Actually, allowing rates to revert to 9.3% would reduce revenue concentration somewhat but not much.

4. Equity/economic efficiency: The tax burden falls on high earners and capital gains. Meanwhile, beneficiaries of the tax cut are the top 2%.

Conversely, losing revenue reduces required school spending automatically, so the discretionary hit is smaller than headline. 1. Is there any credible nonpartisan group opposing on grounds other than ideology (e.g., Bay Area Council, California Chamber of Commerce, PPIC)? Chamber of Commerce? Also possibly some Democrats/moderate business groups? The LA Times said Prop 3 "garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Prop 40" — interesting, so some wealthy interests support Prop 3 as an alternative to Prop 40 (maybe to demonstrate revenue can be raised without a wealth tax; or because of the conflict clause).

2. Check whether there's a concern that Prop 3's conflict clause could nullify Prop 41/42 (which some voters might want). If Prop 3 gets more yes votes than Prop 41 or 42 and they're deemed conflicting (affecting "tax rates for personal income"), Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is null and void. Prop 41 concerns special taxes and Gann limit exemptions; Prop 42 concerns taxes on personal property. Arguably neither "affects the tax rates for personal income," though tax professors suggested Prop 42 could be read to nullify Prop 3 (a conflict). Under the constitutional rule, whichever gets more votes prevails. The "millionaire tax" is back on the California ballot: Proposition 3 would make the 2012 tax rates permanent
Proposition 3 would keep California's top income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% after 2030 instead of letting them drop to 9.3%. The brackets, what it means at $500,000 or $5 million, where the $5 billion to $15 billion goes, and who is paying for the campaign.
by
Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/mac/)
Updated
October 15, 2026

California's high-earner income tax is funding schools and community colleges under Proposition 3, which asks voters in November 2026 to make the 2012 rates permanent.
Proposition 3 would make California's highest income tax rates permanent. Since 2012, California's highest earners have paid 10.3%, 11.3% or 12.3% on the top slices of their income, rates that voters approved as Proposition 30 and extended as Proposition 55. Today those rates start at about $371,000 of taxable income for single filers and about $743,000 for joint filers. Those rates run through the 2030 tax year and then fall back to 9.3%. Prop 3, an initiative constitutional amendment (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/) placed on the ballot by petition, deletes the end date; one of its two proponents is the president of the California Teachers Association. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/), and it leads in both public polls: 58% to 40% in PPIC's September survey and 54% to 34% in UC Berkeley's.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California’s November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure’s rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) The stakes are large and lopsided. The Legislative Analyst's Office estimates Prop 3 keeps $5 billion to $15 billion a year in the state budget, collected from the top 2% of taxpayers, who already pay about half of all state income taxes. Supporters frame a yes vote as no tax increase at all; opponents frame it as the "largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." Both descriptions refer to the same rates. This explainer sets out what the text changes, what the rates mean in dollars, where the money goes (the 89% school figure and the LAO's 40% figure are both right, and measure different things), and who is paying for each side.
Proposition 3 deletes the 2030 end date from the Prop 30 tax rates
The text of proposed law (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf) amends one section of the Constitution, Article XIII, section 36, which is where Prop 30 put the rates in 2012. The edits are deletions of dates:
In the two paragraphs that set the higher rates, the words "and before January 1, 2031" are struck, so the rates apply "for any taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2012" with no end.
The line in each paragraph that says it "shall become inoperative on December 1, 2031" is struck.
In the rules for the Education Protection Account, the fund that receives the money, end years such as "2030" and "2030–31" become "thereafter."
The rates themselves are unchanged. In the Constitution they are written in 2012 dollars: 10.3% on single-filer income over $250,000, 11.3% over $300,000 and 12.3% over $500,000, with parallel brackets for heads of household, all "recomputed" each year for inflation under the state's normal indexing. The Franchise Tax Board's 2025 rate schedules (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-540-tax-rate-schedules.pdf) put those thresholds at $371,479, $445,771 and $742,953 for single filers; $742,958, $891,542 and $1,485,906 for joint filers; and $505,208, $606,251 and $1,010,417 for heads of household. Prop 3 does not touch the separate 1% tax on taxable income above $1 million that voters added for mental health services, now called the Behavioral Health Services Tax. Together the two make California's top marginal rate 13.3% today. If Prop 3 fails, the top rate in 2031 would be 10.3%.
The measure also includes a conflicting-measures clause: if another measure "that affects the tax rates for personal income" is on the same ballot and gets fewer yes votes, Prop 3 prevails "in their entirety" and the other measure is void. The LAO's notes on potential interactions for Props 40, 41 and 42, the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/) and its two countermeasures, do not mention Prop 3.
California income tax rates for top earners are holding at 10.3% to 12.3% under Proposition 3 rather than falling to 9.3% after 2030, with the yearly difference shown at incomes from $400,000 to $5 million in 2026. California income tax rates in dollars: $285 at $400,000, $134,398 at $5 million
The higher rates apply only to the slices of income above each threshold, so their effect starts small and grows quickly. Using the 2025 brackets, we calculated what the Prop 30 rates add to a year's state income tax compared with taxing the same income at 9.3% above the 9.3% threshold. A single filer with $400,000 of taxable income pays $285 more. At $500,000 the difference is $1,828; at $1 million, $14,398; at $5 million, $134,398. Joint filers' brackets are twice as wide: a couple with $500,000 pays nothing extra and a couple with $1 million pays $3,655 more, rising to $28,796 at $2 million and $118,796 at $5 million. These are illustrations at 2025 brackets; by 2031 the thresholds will be higher after inflation indexing.

content.text:
"pay about half of all state income taxes." Because much of their income comes from investments and capital gains, the yield swings with the stock market: "In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion." The state plans about $250 billion in General Fund spending this year, according to the same analysis; our 2026–27 state budget guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/legal/2026-27-california-state-budget-guide/) covers where it goes.
Prop 3's school money: 89% to K–12 schools, and about 40% of the total in practice
Two official figures about where Prop 3's money goes look contradictory and are both accurate. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/title-summary.htm) says the measure "allocates tax revenues 89% to K–12 schools, 11% to community colleges." The LAO says "roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges" and "the rest would go to other state programs," with part set aside in reserves.
The first figure describes the Education Protection Account. Section 36 sends the revenue there and splits it 89% to school districts, county offices and charter schools and 11% to community college districts, as general-purpose money that local boards spend "in open session" and may not use "for salaries or benefits of administrators or any other administrative costs." Each district must publish an annual accounting online, the account is audited, and the Attorney General or a district attorney can seek "civil or criminal penalties" for misuse.
The second figure describes the net effect on the budget. The same section deems the account's revenue "General Fund revenues" for Proposition 98, the constitutional minimum for school and community college funding. The account's money therefore counts toward that minimum rather than adding on top of it, and the state's other spending on schools adjusts around it. The LAO's October 2025 letter (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/fiscal-impact-estimate-report%2825-0016%29.pdf) to the Attorney General puts the result at "typically, about 40 percent." The measure's own findings say as much: the revenue goes to schools, and "State funding is freed up to help balance the budget and provide for a Rainy Day Fund."
Prop 30 in 2012, Prop 55 in 2016, Prop 3 in 2026
Prop 30 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2012-general/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2012 with 7,014,114 votes, 55.4%; it also raised the state sales tax by a quarter cent from 2013 through 2016. Prop 55 passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2016-general/sov/06-sov-summary.pdf) in November 2016 with 8,594,273 votes, 63.3%, extending the income tax rates, but not the sales tax, through 2030. Prop 3 would be the third vote on the same rates and the first without an expiration date. Its findings say the tax "has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other essential services" and that letting it expire "would result in an immediate reduction to state revenues of over $10 billion"; those are the proponents' figures.
Proposition 3's backers and the $46 million campaign
The proponents of record are Benjamin Gevercer and David B. Goldberg, according to the Attorney General's active-measures list (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) (file 25-0016, title and summary issued November 4, 2025). Goldberg signs the ballot argument as president of the California Teachers Association.
The money is almost entirely on one side. The Secretary of State's contribution page (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) for Prop 3 reports $46,260,006 contributed in support through October 6, across four committees, and $5,500 in opposition, to a committee sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association. The FPPC's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 12, puts support from top contributors at $49.7 million. The main Yes committee's largest donors are the California Teachers Association's issues committee ($33.4 million), the National Education Association ($7.5 million), the California School Employees Association ($2.6 million), the California Federation of Teachers ($1.75 million) and SEIU California ($1.5 million). No opposing committee has reached the list's $1 million threshold.
The arguments: "Not a new tax" versus "temporary" taxes made permanent
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/3/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Goldberg, California School Nurses Organization president Katie Nilsson and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California president Jodi Hicks, says "Proposition 3 is NOT a new tax and does NOT raise taxes on anyone" and that without it "millionaires and billionaires" would get "a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities." It says the 8 million public school and community college students "face billions in cuts" without the revenue, and stresses that the money cannot be spent "on bureaucracy or administrative overhead," which the text supports for the Education Protection Account itself.
The No argument, signed by the presidents of the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, says "Politicians told voters higher income taxes would be temporary" and that Prop 3 turns them into "PERMANENTLY higher income taxes." It argues that Californians already pay "the highest income taxes, highest sales taxes and highest gas taxes," that the state "turned a $100 billion budget surplus into a $30 billion budget deficit in just three years," and that "California doesn't have a revenue problem. We have a spending problem." The rebuttal, led by Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association president Jon Coupal, calls the measure "the largest permanent state income tax increase in California history." The deficit and spending figures are the campaign's; all ballot arguments carry the guide's note that they "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Polling and endorsements on Proposition 3
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters found 58% yes, 40% no and 2% undecided. The split is partisan: Democrats 82% to 16% in favor, Republicans 18% to 80% against, independents 57% to 41% in favor. Voters in households earning $100,000 or more backed it 55% to 43%. Asked which of the 14 measures interested them most, 17% named Prop 3. UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf), fielded September 15–20, found 54% yes, 34% no and 13% undecided, a "solid 20-point lead," in contrast with the 45–42 split it found on the Prop 40 billionaire tax.
The California Democratic Party supports (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) Prop 3 and the California Republican Party opposes (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) it. Governor Newsom plans to vote yes, according to the San Francisco Chronicle's account (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of the positions his campaign released on October 9. The supporters listed in the Voter Information Guide are the California Teachers Association, the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California; the opponents listed are the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Proposition 3 after November 3: Permanent rates from 2031, or a return to 9.3%
If Prop 3 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, which is due December 11, but nothing changes on anyone's tax bill: the same rates continue, and the difference first shows up in the 2031 tax year, when they would otherwise have ended. Because the rates would sit in the Constitution, changing them would take another statewide vote. If it fails, the rates still apply through the 2030 tax year, and from 2031 the top rate on income below $1 million becomes 9.3%, and the state budget would lose an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion a year.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, FTB 2025 rate schedules, campaign-finance data as of October 12, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party and governor positions as of October 12, 2026, and polling fielded through September 20, 2026.
